operator_plays.name: Distressed Asset Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Locate mispriced, orphaned, or administratively stranded assets—tax-sale overages, unclaimed state funds, dormant judgments, government surplus lots, or distressed micro-businesses—and capture a contingent recovery fee or acquisition spread.

Unclaimed property & judgment dockets
Surplus auction manifests

Execute skip-tracing or asset inspection to confirm net realizable value
Lock in contingent recovery agreements or below-intrinsic buyouts
metrics: Gross spread / contingent fee per case
Claim approval rate
Days from filing to disbursement

Acquire the codebase, store listing, and domain for $3,000–$35,000 with an escrowed transfer through the official developer console

Post-acquisition review rating stability (>=4.4 stars) and uninstall rate (<3%)

chapters.title: What Exactly Is Business Acquisition?
chapters.subtitle: Cash-Flowing SMB Ownership Through ETA, QoE, SBA Financing, Seller Notes, and Evidence-Led 100-Day Turnarounds
chapters.executive_summary: Business acquisition buys control of an existing operating company and earns money from its delivered products or services, not from the purchase price or customer funds passing through its accounts. Candidate #13, Business Acquisition, holds Rank #17 of 29 and scores 86/100: capital and labor intensity constrain otherwise attractive cash generation. This chapter maps seven operating plays, from distressed_asset_recovery to recurring-contract conversion, and tests each against collections, staffing, transferability, and debt service. Canonical annual owner profit is $60,000 Conservative, $243,750 Base, and $540,000 Scaled, after interest but before principal repayments. Durable ownership requires verified earnings, retained customer relationships, transferable operating rights, and back-office automation that strengthens controls rather than disguising missing people.

sections.heading: 1. Buy an operating system, not a seller's income claim
paragraphs: Business acquisition is the purchase of assets or equity that gives a buyer control over an existing company's productive resources, customer obligations, and earning capacity. Entrepreneurship through acquisition, or ETA, replaces the startup's search for initial demand with a search for transferable cash flow. Micro-private-equity ownership applies similar discipline to smaller companies, often with one operating manager rather than a portfolio bureaucracy. The buyer pays for equipment, working capital, relationships, intellectual property, and goodwill; those payments are investments, not operating revenue. An asset purchase selects assets and assumed obligations through the agreement, but does not automatically eliminate statutory successor exposure. An equity purchase generally leaves the company and its historical obligations intact while changing its owners. Neither structure substitutes for tax, employment, environmental, licensing, and contract diligence. Begin with a transaction perimeter: which entity invoices, which entity employs, which contracts transfer, which deposits remain owed, and which liabilities survive closing. Put that perimeter beside the purchase agreement and opening balance sheet. A profitable business that loses its qualifying license, landlord permission, or indispensable customer upon transfer is not the same business the seller marketed. Price the operation that can legally and practically continue, not the historical operation that existed under someone else's relationships.

Recognized operator revenue follows the acquired company's customer performance, not the amount financed or the volume of other people's money it handles. Under an accrual reporting policy, record service revenue as contracted performance occurs and product revenue when the relevant control-transfer conditions are met. Cash-basis tax records may differ, so reconcile them rather than treating deposits as earned sales. A property manager collecting $200,000 monthly rent at an 8% management fee ordinarily has $16,000 monthly management revenue, not $200,000 of company sales. A reseller controlling inventory before delivery may instead report gross product sales with corresponding cost of goods sold; a marketplace agent may report only its commission. Assess the actual principal-agent relationship, not the software's gross-volume dashboard. Customer retainers, refundable deposits, sales taxes collected for authorities, acquisition loans, and owner capital require separate balance-sheet treatment. Buying a company for $1,200,000 does not create $1,200,000 revenue. Build a bridge from signed orders to delivered work, invoices, credit notes, processor settlements, and bank receipts. QuickBooks Online or Xero can hold the ledger, but the operator must define the recognition policy and investigate settlement differences rather than silently booking every bank credit as sales.

The canonical scorecard describes acquired business sales and margin after interest, before principal repayments. Conservative sales of $750,000 at 8% produce $60,000 annual owner profit; Base sales of $1,875,000 at 13.0% produce $243,750; Scaled sales of $3,000,000 at 18% produce $540,000. The first two cases require seven full-time employees plus three contractors, while Scaled requires eight employees plus four contractors. Twelve people is a real management system, not a passive-income side project. These cases imply $690,000, $1,631,250, and $2,460,000 respectively of costs and charges within the stated profit boundary. Treat the separate $6,000-$25,000 monthly opex planning range as a scope-dependent budget input, not a complete expense reconciliation. Startup capital of $30,000-$120,000 must cover the actual equity requirement, transaction spending, liquidity reserve, and unfunded transition work; first-deal timing is six to eighteen months. Principal amortization, capital purchases, and working-capital expansion can consume profit without reducing that scorecard measure. Build a second cash waterfall for those uses. The 86/100 score reflects this burden: revenue potential contributes 24 points, margin 16, team efficiency seven, startup accessibility two, and automation eight. The opportunity is operating ownership with leverage, not an accounting shortcut.

sections.heading: 2. Screen sub-verticals for transferable demand and controllable delivery
paragraphs: Choose a sub-vertical by its renewal mechanics and operating dependencies, not by a listing broker's favorite multiple. BizBuySell, Axial, and Acquire.com can surface opportunities, but marketplace presence is neither earnings verification nor proof of transferability. Ask what customers actually repurchase, who performs the work, and what happens when the founder stops answering calls. Commercial cleaning can retain recurring sites yet lose its margin through overtime and contract underbidding. HVAC maintenance can build route density yet depend on a qualifying license holder. A managed IT provider can show monthly recurring revenue while harboring underpriced support obligations and unsupported infrastructure. Compare businesses using gross profit after direct delivery labor, customer-level retention, collection timing, service backlog, and replacement management cost. Revenue per employee alone rewards outsourcing and pass-through sales without proving operating quality. Obtain twelve to twenty-four months of invoice-line exports and group customers by acquisition cohort, location, service type, and technician. Then ask which margin disappears if the top customer, seller, or key employee leaves. A durable small-team moat consists of repeatable performance and accumulated operational knowledge that the buyer can retain, teach, and inspect without requiring the founder's daily intervention.

The comparison matrix uses named operating systems to make diligence concrete; its fee descriptions are customer-contract structures, not asserted software subscription prices. Request actual vendor agreements, seat counts, payment-processing schedules, implementation obligations, and change-of-control terms. A platform migration can destroy dispatch history, maintenance reminders, or customer-specific pricing if the acquisition team treats exports as an afterthought. Preserve a read-only source archive and reconcile opening balances before replacing software. Test customer concentration against contribution profit, not merely sales: losing one complex account can improve economics, while losing a high-margin anchor can strand an entire crew. Examine contract assignment, cancellation rights, service credits, warranties, and customer security requirements. For a franchise resale, verify franchisor transfer requirements and evaluate disclosure obligations under 16 CFR Part 436 where applicable; a familiar brand does not make the territory freely transferable. For government contractors, determine whether an asset transfer requires federal recognition through the FAR Subpart 42.12 novation process. Equity changes and asset transfers do not necessarily receive identical treatment. Preserve the specific customer permission, vendor support, and operating authorization that produces cash rather than assuming goodwill moves automatically with the purchase price.

Durability also requires distinguishing collectible contracts from contractual headlines. A three-year agreement with convenient termination rights can be economically weaker than a month-to-month relationship supported by measurable switching costs. Inspect cancellation cohorts, concessions, chargebacks, aged receivables, and post-period credits before assigning a recurring-revenue premium. For software, examine repository ownership, administrator access, hosting bills, dependency licenses, and support hours per account. For physical services, inspect truck condition, spare-parts availability, workers' compensation history, and actual payroll classifications. Federal wage-and-hour obligations under 29 U.S.C. 206 and 207 are concrete cost inputs where applicable, not items to remove through aggressive add-backs. State requirements may impose additional costs. Quality of Earnings, or QoE, should connect reported profit to sustainable delivery economics rather than simply produce a normalized earnings number. Require a written exception log showing the source, proposed adjustment, cash consequence, responsible reviewer, and purchase-agreement response. An unresolved exception must change price, structure, reserves, or the decision to proceed. When the seller cannot substantiate claimed renewals, underwrite documented collections and demonstrated retention. A lower valuation supported by evidence is more useful than a sophisticated model built on customers who can disappear immediately after closing.

callout.body: Experienced acquirers test transferability through source records, retained people, and customer behavior before paying for claimed recurring earnings.

sections.heading: 3. Map seven operating plays to measurable economics and bounded fallbacks
paragraphs: This chapter maps seven plays: the specified distressed_asset_recovery TRACK_1 play and six descriptive acquisition operating mappings shown below. The latter are chapter labels, not additional canonical catalog identifiers. All play-level figures are illustrative incremental economics, not replacements for the volume's three annual cases. Distressed asset recovery locates mispriced or administratively stranded value, including distressed micro-businesses, government surplus, dormant judgments, tax-sale overages, and state unclaimed funds. These are different legal and operational lanes, not interchangeable claims. An authorized $80,000 recovery with a legally permitted 15% contingent fee yields $12,000 fee revenue; $4,000 of direct case costs leaves $8,000 before overhead and tax effects. The $80,000 claimant principal is not operator revenue. Buying transferable surplus equipment for $18,000, spending $4,000 on transport and repair, and selling it for $30,000 produces $8,000 gross spread before other costs. Verify title, liens, redemption rights, fee restrictions, waiting periods, and claimant authority for the applicable jurisdiction. The fallback is diversified multi-state docket sourcing and attorney-backed filing partnerships where required, with state-specific procedures rather than copied forms. Diversification never cures an invalid claim or authorizes work reserved to licensed professionals.

The recurring-service acquisition play starts with retained customers rather than new-sales assumptions: 100 commercial accounts paying $500 monthly generate $600,000 annual sales, and a 30% direct contribution margin yields $180,000 before central overhead, financing, and other charges. If retention cannot be verified, reduce the price or use a properly documented retention adjustment rather than borrowing against the seller's forecast. The seller succession play purchases operating continuity from a retiring owner. Replacing $90,000 of genuinely removable owner compensation with $70,000 of manager compensation creates only $20,000 incremental annual improvement, not a $90,000 add-back; employer costs can narrow it further. If no competent manager will stay, retain the seller through a defined transition or defer the transaction. The route-density tuck-in play acquires adjacent demand that existing supervision can absorb. Saving 20 paid travel hours weekly at $30 loaded hourly cost across 50 weeks creates $30,000 potential annual labor savings. Confirm overtime, crew availability, and service windows before counting them. If customer locations do not fit, operate the acquired route separately and underwrite standalone costs. Each play must survive its fallback without requiring speculative revenue growth to pay scheduled debt service.

The working-capital repair play improves cash conversion rather than pretending collections are new profit. At $1,875,000 annual credit sales using a 365-day convention, reducing receivable days from 50 to 40 releases approximately $51,370 of cash once, assuming steady sales and collectible balances. If disputed invoices resist collection, repair documentation and tighten future terms instead of coercing customers or booking fictitious recoveries. The back-office integration play consolidates reporting and administration: eliminating $2,400 monthly duplicated costs while adding $900 monthly support creates $18,000 annual recurring savings. A $12,000 migration expense leaves $6,000 first-year benefit before other effects; retain parallel reporting until balances reconcile. The recurring-contract conversion play turns demonstrated repeat demand into properly scoped service agreements. Converting 200 willing customers to $40 monthly plans adds $96,000 annual contracted sales if every plan remains active; $36,000 direct fulfillment costs leave $60,000 contribution before other charges. Prepayments still represent future service obligations where performance remains outstanding. If attachment or renewal disappoints, keep profitable one-off work and stop subsidizing uneconomic plans. Do not add these examples together and call the sum the Base case: overlaps, implementation timing, staffing, and financing determine which improvements can coexist.

sections.heading: 4. Reconcile debt, diligence, and the first 100 days before closing
paragraphs: Finance the acquisition around verified downside cash flow, not the maximum loan someone will discuss. SBA-backed acquisition financing remains subject to eligibility, credit analysis, current program requirements, and lender underwriting; 13 CFR 120.110 identifies ineligible business categories and 13 CFR 120.150 addresses lending criteria. Obtain the lender's written treatment of equity injection, seller debt, standby arrangements, guarantees, and distributions before relying on a proposed structure. A seller note does not automatically satisfy equity requirements or permit immediate payments. Model interest within the scorecard margin and principal below it, avoiding double subtraction. With illustrative annual principal of $48,000 and maintenance capital spending of $20,000, the three canonical profits leave negative $8,000, positive $175,750, and positive $472,000 respectively before working-capital changes and any other cash items outside the scorecard boundary. Those amounts are cash sensitivity outputs, not revised canonical profits. Debt-service coverage uses the lender's defined cash-flow numerator and total required debt service; do not substitute owner profit without a reconciliation. Stress collection delays, a lost anchor customer, higher borrowing costs where applicable, and manager replacement. Maintain a funded liquidity reserve rather than treating an undrawn or uncommitted credit discussion as available cash.

Convert diligence findings into closing mechanics. Agree the working-capital definition and peg, excluding cash, debt, and other items exactly as the purchase agreement specifies; examine seasonality and stale inventory before using a trailing average. Trace customer deposits to remaining fulfillment costs so the buyer does not inherit service obligations without funding. In a qualifying asset acquisition, coordinate purchase-price allocation under 26 U.S.C. 1060 and the applicable Form 8594 reporting requirements; separately model amortization of qualifying acquired intangibles under 26 U.S.C. 197. Tax deductions do not eliminate the initial cash purchase. Obtain lien searches, payoff letters, release documentation, lease permissions, license continuity plans, and required customer consents. Inspect payroll tax filings and worker classifications, then reconcile accrued wages, vacation obligations, and benefits according to applicable law and the transaction documents. Negotiate representations, indemnity limits, escrow, and earnout definitions around identified risks, recognizing that contractual recourse is only as useful as its enforceability and collectibility. A seller's promise to fix accounting later should become a dated deliverable with a measurable closing consequence. Keep a single issues register linking every unresolved finding to cash exposure, responsible ownership, and the final agreement.

The first 100 days should preserve the revenue engine before attempting a turnaround. During days one through thirty, retain key employees, contact priority customers, validate bank permissions, reconcile opening balances, and run a rolling thirteen-week cash forecast. Confirm that payroll, insurance, licenses, supplier accounts, and emergency service coverage work under the new ownership. During days thirty-one through sixty, eliminate billing leakage, repair purchasing controls, and publish weekly operational metrics with named owners. During days sixty-one through one hundred, implement only improvements supported by measured capacity and customer feedback. Automate financial reporting and back-office workflows through controlled integrations, not shared administrator credentials or unreviewed payment instructions. Separate vendor creation, payment preparation, and payment release wherever staffing permits, with independent review where roles must overlap. Monitor retained revenue, direct contribution, overtime, receivable days, callbacks, and covenant headroom together. A revenue increase with slower collections and more rework may indicate deterioration rather than progress. Review the acquisition thesis monthly against the original downside case. Durable small-team ownership is visible in reliable reporting, repeatable delivery, and management depth; fragile beginner hype depends on aggressive add-backs, perpetual refinancing, and the founder quietly continuing to perform work nobody included in the budget.

chapters.executive_summary: Business Acquisition is Candidate #13, Rank #17 of 29, with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 86/100. The buyer funds ownership; customers fund the operating business; neither borrowed principal nor escrow releases create operating revenue. This chapter maps seven operator plays across application acquisitions, recurring services, maintenance, distribution, route businesses, milestone contracts, and receivables recovery. It identifies who controls each budget, what makes payment urgent, and which settlement conditions protect cash without obstructing delivery. Canonical annual owner profits are $60,000 Conservative, $243,750 Base, and $540,000 Scaled, after interest and before principal repayments. Use verified authority, customer retention evidence, controlled disbursements, and a thirteen-week cash forecast to prevent an attractive purchase price from becoming an unfunded operating obligation.

sections.heading: 1. Separate the ownership check from the customer check
paragraphs: Start every acquisition with two payment maps, not one purchase price. The ownership map identifies the buyer entity, equity contributors, acquisition lender, seller, escrow agent, and creditors receiving payoff wires. The operating map identifies customers, budget owners, purchasing administrators, invoice approvers, and the accounts-payable team that actually releases cash. A seller may accept a lower headline price for retirement certainty, a short transition, or release from personal guarantees; none of those motives makes customers more willing to renew. Customers pay because the acquired company keeps equipment running, fulfills orders, preserves productive workflows, or completes a measurable deliverable. Interview both the economic buyer and the payment administrator before assigning value to a customer relationship. Ask who can authorize an annual commitment, which purchase-order fields must match, when the next budget cycle begins, and whether a change of control requires notice or permission. Record actual contract language rather than assuming that an asset sale transfers every agreement. A procurement manager's enthusiasm cannot substitute for an authorized signature, a valid assignment, or an invoice that the customer's accounting system will accept.

Budget authority is especially important when apparent urgency comes from a statutory obligation. Payroll funding, tax deposits, license renewal, and lien releases have deadlines, but those deadlines do not automatically give your company a collectible claim against somebody else. Under 26 U.S.C. 7501, withheld taxes are held in trust; 26 U.S.C. 6672 can impose personal liability on responsible persons for willful failures involving covered trust-fund taxes. Inspect payroll tax records, deposit evidence, and correspondence rather than accepting a seller's statement that the payroll provider handles everything. For an applicable asset acquisition, reconcile purchase-price allocation with the reporting framework in 26 U.S.C. 1060 and Form 8594. Investigate state successor-tax procedures and occupational licenses for the actual operating jurisdictions. These obligations influence the closing reserve, transaction structure, and buyer's willingness to fund; they are not additional sales. Have the purchase agreement identify who supplies each clearance, who pays each existing liability, and what happens when evidence arrives late. Protect operating liquidity by separating ordinary working capital from amounts reserved for identified preclosing exposures.

Translate the scorecard into collection targets before negotiating leverage. Conservative sales of $750,000 at 8% produce $60,000 annual owner net profit; Base sales of $1,875,000 at 13.0% produce $243,750; Scaled sales of $3,000,000 at 18% produce $540,000. These margins are after interest and before principal repayments. The first two cases use seven full-time employees and three contractors; Scaled uses eight and four. Monthly sales equivalents are $62,500, $156,250, and $250,000, while monthly profit equivalents are $5,000, $20,312.50, and $45,000. Those are arithmetic averages, not a seasonal cash forecast. For example, an illustrative $100,000 annual principal schedule would leave $143,750 from Base profit before other cash adjustments, including working-capital investment and capital expenditure. It does not revise the canonical profit figure. Reconcile QuickBooks Online or Xero sales to bank deposits, processor reports, receivables aging, and deferred-revenue schedules. Exclude acquisition borrowing, investor contributions, seller-note principal, customer pass-through funds, and refundable deposits from earned sales. Use the stated $30,000–$120,000 startup range and $6,000–$25,000 monthly operating-expense range as planning parameters, not substitutes for a target-specific cost bridge that actually supports these margins.

sections.heading: 2. Match the settlement mechanism to the obligation being paid
paragraphs: The eight mechanisms in the matrix solve different problems: wire and ACH move money, escrow controls release, retainers change payment timing, statutory disbursement follows a legally defined allocation, platform checkout combines authorization and collection, factoring finances receivables, and milestone holds reserve consideration against performance. Treating all eight as interchangeable payment rails hides ownership and reversal risk. For closing, prepare a sources-and-uses schedule that balances buyer equity, lender proceeds, seller financing, purchase consideration, debt payoffs, expenses, and opening cash. A seller note is a financing source without necessarily creating a cash movement at closing. Obtain payoff statements with expiration dates and per-diem interest, then pair each payoff with the required lien-release process. Confirm beneficiary details through a known telephone number established independently of the latest email thread. Require two authorized people to approve changes to stored payment instructions. Under the applicable state enactment of UCC Article 4A, payment-order authorization and agreed security procedures matter; a wire transfer is not buyer protection merely because the bank accepted the instruction. Retain the bank reference, recipient confirmation, and final closing statement together.

An escrow agreement must name the holder, bank-account arrangements, release evidence, objection period, permitted deductions, and dispute procedure. Distinguish money reserved for seller indemnity from working capital that the operating company needs immediately. For example, a $50,000 illustrative holdback on a $500,000 purchase leaves $450,000 of purchase consideration available for immediate seller distribution before other deductions; neither amount is acquired-business revenue. A milestone release should depend on observable events such as an accepted customer assignment or delivery of administrator access, not the buyer's subjective satisfaction. Statutory disbursement is relevant only where a specific regime applies. In a federal contracting acquisition, FAR 42.1204 addresses novation agreements; transfer of a contractor's assets does not simply redirect government payments to a new entity. Federal contract payment assignments also require analysis under 31 U.S.C. 3727 and 41 U.S.C. 6305. Verify the contracting officer's process and the applicable exceptions before treating assigned receipts as available collateral. For ordinary private transactions, do not invent a statutory escrow requirement where the purchase agreement and relevant state rules control.

For operating receipts, price the actual collection cost and cash delay rather than quoting a rail's advertised speed. An illustrative $10,000 card sale with a contracted 2.9% plus $0.30 processing charge creates a $290.30 expense and $9,709.70 settlement before reserves, refunds, or taxes. Generally, record earned gross sales and the processing expense separately when the business is the principal; merchant gross merchandise volume processed for others is not automatically its revenue. Stripe or Shopify Payments balances can remain subject to payout reserves and disputes. Business ACH arrangements require valid authorization and applicable network procedures; consumer recurring debits also require attention to 12 CFR 1005.10. A bank posting alone does not establish that every return risk has expired. Retainers for future work usually create a performance obligation until earned, while factoring supplies financing or receivable-sale proceeds rather than a second sale. Reconcile invoices, clearing accounts, fees, reversals, reserves, and deposits daily during transition. Maintain a second collection option for customers whose purchasing rules prevent card payment, and test new banking details before retiring the seller's authorized collection arrangement.

sections.heading: 3. Underwrite counterparties and protect fees before delivery
paragraphs: Screen the seller, customers, lenders, and intermediaries separately because each can break a different part of the cash chain. For the seller, reconcile legal ownership to organizational records, lien searches, tax documentation, and actual control of critical accounts. Search the appropriate secretary of state filing system for UCC financing statements, then obtain underlying security documents and current payoff evidence; a search result alone does not establish lien priority or a clean release. Use PACER for relevant federal litigation and bankruptcy records, supplemented by state court sources and direct explanations. For customers, request trade references, payment history, disputes, concentration reports, and evidence of their ability to absorb the next delivery. Dun & Bradstreet or Experian Business reports are inputs, not replacements for invoice-level verification. Ask the top ten customers to confirm balances through a controlled process with the seller's permission, avoiding disclosure of transaction terms beyond the authorized scope. Investigate credits issued after period end, extended payment promises, and unusually large invoices immediately before marketing the business. These can inflate apparent earnings without improving collectible cash.

Set exposure limits from cash at risk, not from relationship warmth. Suppose a customer buys $20,000 monthly and pays sixty days after invoicing; steady receivables exposure is roughly $40,000 before disputes and timing effects. A $15,000 collection limit therefore requires deposits, shorter terms, smaller releases, or a documented exception funded by available liquidity. At Base annual sales, reducing collection time by ten days across a uniformly earned, fully credit-based sales book releases approximately $51,370, calculated as $1,875,000 divided by 365 and multiplied by ten. That is working-capital release, not incremental profit, and the actual benefit depends on eligible receivables and collection behavior. Underwrite factoring on total proceeds: an illustrative $100,000 eligible invoice with an 85% advance supplies $85,000 initially; a $2,000 fee leaves $13,000 from the reserve after full collection, absent other deductions. Recourse can return the loss to the acquired company. Identify whether existing lender documents permit receivable sales and additional liens. Never sell the same invoice twice or conceal a factoring notice from the customer or senior lender.

Fee protection starts with a signed engagement and objective earning event, not a broad threat against circumvention. A buy-side sourcing adviser should document the client entity, introduced target list, covered transaction types, fee formula, payment timing, limited tail, and treatment of preexisting relationships. An illustrative engagement can specify a $5,000 retainer credited against a $25,000 earned closing fee, leaving $20,000 payable at closing; this is adviser compensation, not acquired-company sales. Escrow pays that balance only with valid instructions and any required lender permission. The operator should not promise that a contractual tail overcomes licensing restrictions. Transaction-based compensation involving securities requires examination of 15 U.S.C. 78o, including the conditions and exclusions of the M&A broker exemption in subsection (b)(13), plus applicable state requirements. For ordinary customer services, tie fees to signed scope, delivery records, acceptance windows, and an agreed dispute process. Preserve collection rights without taking unauthorized control of customer accounts or interrupting unrelated services. Use smaller prepaid work packages when credit evidence fails rather than hoping a stronger invoice footer will collect an insolvent customer's balance.

sections.heading: 4. Map seven operating plays into a funded hundred-day transition
paragraphs: The seven chapter mappings below comprise the supplied application-acquisition play and six descriptive acquisition operating plays; the latter are local labels, not additional catalog identifiers. For expired_chrome_extension_acquisitions, scan the Chrome Web Store, WordPress Plugin Directory, and Shopify App Store for neglected utilities with 10,000–250,000 active users and ratings of at least 4.5 stars. Distinguish active users from cumulative installations and verify monetizable engagement with authorized analytics. With 20,000 active users, a hypothetical 2% paid conversion at $8 monthly yields 400 subscribers and $38,400 annual subscription sales. If incremental hosting, support, refunds, platform charges, and maintenance total $18,400, potential annual cash flow is $20,000 before acquisition financing and owner-level taxes. A 1–2x potential cash-flow purchase thesis implies $20,000–$40,000, but unproven conversion calls for staged consideration rather than an unconditional valuation claim. Verify each platform's current ownership-transfer and billing requirements before funding. Keep permissions narrow, grandfather every legacy free feature, and sell additive Pro workflows or explicitly chosen contextual partner offers. Never introduce hidden tracking or background advertising scripts to force the forecast to work.

For the other six mappings, the payer's measurable benefit determines both the price structure and the fallback. A recurring-service customer buys predictable response capacity; a maintenance customer buys less downtime; a distributor's customer buys available inventory; a route customer buys reliable scheduled fulfillment. A project customer buys accepted milestones, while receivables recovery collects existing obligations instead of manufacturing new sales. The matrix's unit calculations are independent illustrations, not an additive portfolio or replacement for the canonical scenarios. Test whether billed units survived the seller's personal involvement and whether contracts permit the intended transfer. For maintenance, distinguish advance collections from earned service revenue. For distribution, separate inventory purchases and supplier terms from customer gross profit. For route businesses, inspect missed-stop credits and driver substitution costs. For milestone work, obtain dated acceptance records before forecasting the next release. Across every mapping, include interest in the operating profit bridge and show scheduled principal separately in the cash forecast. A service business that appears profitable before its seller's unpaid labor is replaced has not yet demonstrated the scorecard's owner economics.

Build the hundred-day transition around collection continuity rather than a simultaneous replacement of every system. Before closing, export authorized customer, vendor, invoice, and subscription records and reconcile opening balances to the agreed working-capital schedule. During days one through ten, confirm customer notices, bank signers, payroll funding, administrator access, and the first settlement batch. During days eleven through thirty, clear billing exceptions, verify top-customer retention, and test the daily cash reconciliation. During days thirty-one through sixty, automate invoice reminders and reporting in QuickBooks Online or Xero while retaining review of changed bank details and unusual credits. During days sixty-one through one hundred, adjust pricing only where contract rights, measured customer value, and support capacity justify it. The acquisition pipeline itself may take six to eighteen months before the first deal; this transition clock starts at ownership transfer, not initial outreach. Report sales, after-interest profit, principal paid, receivable days, customer losses, and unrestricted cash as separate measures. Escalate a missed payroll forecast or covenant breach immediately instead of hiding it inside a favorable monthly revenue chart.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #13, Business Acquisition, ranks #17 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 86/100: attractive cash generation requires substantial capital and operating labor. The canonical annual owner-profit cases are $60,000 Conservative, $243,750 Base, and $540,000 Scaled, after interest but before principal repayments. Seven mapped operating plays connect QoE revenue scrubbing, acquisition pricing, delivery labor, receivables collection, debt structuring, the 100-day turnaround, and Chapter 11 trade-claim purchases. This chapter converts those plays into cohort economics, explicit deductions, cash-conversion requirements, and failure responses. Illustrative cost allocations reconcile exactly to the scorecard without counting acquired assets, customer principal, or purchased claim face amounts as operating sales. The decisive test is cash remaining after principal, maintenance investment, and incremental working capital.

sections.heading: 1. Rebuild acquired revenue into a reconciled cohort waterfall
paragraphs: Start with acquired operating-company sales, not purchase price, enterprise value, customer transaction volume, or financing proceeds. For comparability, define one cohort unit as a completed job producing $1,000 of recognized revenue after customer credits. The Conservative, Base, and Scaled cases therefore contain 750, 1,875, and 3,000 annual job equivalents. Illustrative gross billings are $1,040 per equivalent, with $40 deducted for contractual credits, refunds, and expected revenue reversals. That deduction equals 3.846% of gross billings, not 4% of billings. Annual recognized sales reconcile to $750,000, $1,875,000, and $3,000,000 exactly. In an agency business, replace the job measure with earned commissions and keep customer principal outside revenue. Build the source bridge from QuickBooks Online or NetSuite invoices, credit memos, bank deposits, and Stripe settlement exports. Match customer identifiers and service dates before grouping cohorts. A deposit proves cash movement, not completed performance; an invoice proves a billing event, not collectibility. Separate sales-tax collections, customer deposits, and purchased receivables from current-period earned sales. Require the monthly revenue bridge to explain timing differences rather than forcing deposits to equal sales through miscellaneous journal entries. Preserve source exports so subsequent collections can validate the original acquisition underwriting.

The waterfall below supplies illustrative deductions because the canonical scorecard specifies endpoints, not a detailed chart of accounts. Materials and fulfillment inputs consume $225,000, $525,000, and $780,000. Loaded employee delivery labor consumes $280,000, $520,000, and $720,000; contractor delivery labor consumes $60,000, $150,000, and $240,000. Employee allocations include payroll taxes and benefits, while contractor allocations require completed deliverables and verified invoices. The resulting direct contribution is $185,000, $680,000, and $1,260,000 before customer acquisition and overhead. Budget customer acquisition at $20,000, $60,000, and $90,000 and operating overhead at $65,000, $210,000, and $390,000. These allocations produce EBITDA of $100,000, $410,000, and $780,000. Deduct depreciation and amortization of $10,000, $31,250, and $60,000, then interest of $30,000, $135,000, and $180,000. Annual owner profit lands exactly at $60,000, $243,750, and $540,000. Treat these as pass-through operating cases without an entity-level income-tax expense; owner personal taxes remain outside the model. A different tax structure requires a separate bridge. Do not describe this residual as spendable distributions: principal, capital investment, and working-capital changes still consume cash after the profit calculation. The allocation is an underwriting hypothesis to replace with verified target-company records, not evidence about an actual seller.

Use seven operating plays to organize execution. Six chapter-local labels describe QoE revenue scrubbing, acquisition pricing, delivery-labor control, receivables collection, debt structuring, and the 100-day turnaround; the supplied mapped identifier is chapter11_trade_claim_convenience_class_rollup. These labels do not imply additional catalog identifiers. QoE scrubbing tests whether the $40 credit allowance captures actual subsequent credits; under-reserving requires a price adjustment or funded reserve. Acquisition pricing connects sustainable earnings to purchase consideration rather than treating borrowed money as income. Delivery control compares contractor cost of $80 per job across all three cases against rework and acceptance evidence. Receivables collection measures days to usable cash, including processor restrictions. Debt structuring separates interest expense from principal cash requirements. The turnaround play assigns owners to collection, retention, and procurement improvements before assuming margin expansion. The trade-claim play uses a separate investment ledger because a purchased receivable is not a sale by the acquired operating company. At Base, owner profit is $130 per job; at Conservative it is $80, and at Scaled it is $180. Any improvement proposal must identify which deduction changes, when cash moves, and what operating evidence supports the change. Reject plans that count the same payroll reduction both as a seller add-back and a future saving.

callout.title: Find the deductions that survive a seller's presentation
callout.body: Reconstruct each adjustment from operational evidence before capitalizing it into purchase price.
items: Sample credit memos issued during the first 90 days after each historical quarter; attribute them to original job cohorts rather than the issue month alone.
Trace five large contractor invoices to accepted jobs and subsequent customer credits; repeat visits frequently reveal delivery costs hidden in general administration.
Demand a replacement-role budget for every owner compensation add-back; remove only the portion exceeding verified replacement cost.
Reconcile processor gross collections, fees, refunds, disputes, and restricted balances separately; a settlement deposit is neither gross sales nor unrestricted earnings.

sections.heading: 2. Price retention, delivery capacity, and debt before paying for growth
paragraphs: Customer acquisition cost means the cost to win customers, not the price to acquire the company. The illustrative budgets purchase 100, 250, and 375 new customers, giving CAC of $200, $240, and $240. Assuming each new customer buys two $1,000 jobs within twelve months, recognized first-year customer revenue is $2,000. Before fixed employee payroll, materials and contractor deductions leave $620, $640, and $660 per job. Two jobs therefore generate $1,240, $1,280, and $1,320 of marginal contribution, or $1,040, $1,040, and $1,080 after CAC. These figures are not owner profit and are usable only when existing employee capacity can absorb the work. Including allocated employee delivery labor reduces two-job contribution after CAC to approximately $293, $485, and $600 before overhead, depreciation, and interest. Track both views so a busy schedule does not conceal a poor fully loaded return. HubSpot acquisition-source cohorts should reconcile to invoiced jobs, while payroll or timekeeping exports establish available capacity. If customers buy only once, cut projected lifetime contribution rather than borrowing an industry retention assumption. Pause channels with negative fully loaded cohort contribution and retain existing customers before expanding acquisition spending. Charge sales commissions consistently to CAC instead of also burying them in overhead.

Acquisition pricing needs its own sources-and-uses schedule. An illustrative Base transaction pays $1,200,000 for a cash-free, debt-free operating business with normal working capital delivered at closing. Fund that price with $900,000 of acquisition debt and $300,000 of buyer equity, then separately fund $75,000 of transaction expenses and $135,785 of opening liquidity. Buyer cash totals $510,785; the price already includes the negotiated working-capital peg, so adding the peg again would double-count funding. Average debt of $900,000 at an illustrative blended 15% annual rate produces the Base interest deduction of $135,000. This is a modeling assumption, not a quoted SBA rate or an assertion that a particular loan qualifies. Seller-note standby, amortization, permitted uses, and security priorities must match executed documents and lender requirements. Assuming $108,000 annual principal and $31,250 maintenance investment, Base cash after debt service and maintenance is $135,750 before working-capital changes and owner taxes. The bridge adds back $31,250 of noncash expense before subtracting equal maintenance spending. An asset acquisition also requires a supported purchase-price allocation under 26 U.S.C. 1060 where applicable; book expense, tax amortization, and cash investment need separate schedules. If lender proceeds shrink, reduce consideration or increase committed equity before signing.

Stress the same economic system rather than inventing a second optimistic model. A 10% sales loss, with only materials and contractors flexing proportionally, reduces annual profit to $13,500 Conservative, $123,750 Base, and $342,000 Scaled. Employee payroll, CAC, overhead, depreciation, and interest remain fixed in this test. An additional reversal expense equal to one percentage point of baseline recognized sales reduces profit to $52,500, $225,000, and $510,000, assuming no cost recovery. A two-percentage-point interest increase on average debt balances of $300,000, $900,000, and $1,200,000 removes another $6,000, $18,000, and $24,000 respectively. Run these separately first, then combine them without assuming every exposure is independent. For the 100-day turnaround, a one-percentage-point materials reduction at Base saves $18,750 annually only after supplier pricing and service quality support the change. With $5,000 implementation expense, first-year improvement becomes $13,750 before timing effects. If the cheaper input increases refunds, stop substitution and restore the approved specification. The Scaled case's eight employees and four contractors are twelve people, not twelve interchangeable full-time positions. Require actual shift capacity, skill coverage, and employment classification evidence before assigning growth to automation. Reporting automation saves reconciliation effort; it does not manufacture delivery capacity.

callout.title: Verify the four bridges before committing acquisition equity
callout.body: Proceed only when documentary evidence connects revenue, labor, financing, and opening cash.

Replace seller labor add-backs with documented market replacement costs and verify the seven-plus-three or eight-plus-four staffing plan.
Obtain the actual amortization schedule, variable-rate terms, seller-note restrictions, and covenant definitions; calculate coverage using those definitions.
Confirm the working-capital peg, excluded balances, processor restrictions, and available opening liquidity in the executed sources-and-uses schedule.

sections.heading: 3. Fund the gap between earned sales and usable cash
paragraphs: Model working capital from the balance sheet and a weekly cash forecast, not from the income statement alone. Base DSO of 45 days produces receivables of $231,164 on $1,875,000 annual recognized sales. Inventory of 20 days on $525,000 annual materials cost requires $28,767; supplier terms of 30 days provide $43,151 of payable funding. Net operating working capital is approximately $216,781 using unrounded calculations. This simplified peg includes receivables plus inventory less trade payables; the purchase agreement must address accrued payroll, customer deposits, prepaid expenses, and other operating balances explicitly. Conservative assumptions of 30 DSO, 15 inventory days, and 25 payable days produce approximately $55,479. Scaled assumptions of 35 DSO, 15 inventory days, and 30 payable days produce approximately $255,616. These are illustrative steady-state requirements, not additions to revenue or deductions from annual profit. A closing shortfall against the delivered peg changes the purchase adjustment and immediate funding requirement. Inspect aged receivables for disputes and inventory for obsolescence before accepting their book values. A seller can deliver the nominal peg with unusable assets unless eligibility rules, valuation policies, and the true-up mechanism are specified. Agree those definitions before headline price becomes emotionally or contractually difficult to change.

Receivables collection and processor availability are different clocks. Under a stated convention that DSO ends at customer payment, a seven-day settlement lock on 20% of Base sales adds $7,192 of restricted settlement funding. If the accounting DSO already runs through bank availability, do not add those days again. A 15-day DSO deterioration adds $30,822 Conservative, $77,055 Base, and $123,288 Scaled. Base opening liquidity of $135,785 combines the $77,055 delay buffer, $7,192 settlement lock, and $51,538 for two biweekly employee-and-contractor payment cycles. The payment-cycle calculation uses $670,000 annual delivery labor divided by 26 and multiplied by two; actual contractor payment terms should replace that simplifying convention. This reserve is additional to delivered normal working capital and excludes transaction fees. The quoted $6,000-$25,000 monthly operating expense range cannot stand in for total modeled cash outflow: Base materials, delivery labor, CAC, and overhead total approximately $122,083 monthly before interest and principal. Use the detailed waterfall for liquidity planning rather than silently capping expenses at the benchmark range. Negotiate supplier terms without assuming suppliers will finance a change of control. Suspend discretionary distributions whenever the forecast consumes the protected liquidity floor.

Maintain a thirteen-week direct cash forecast with weekly beginning cash, customer receipts, supplier payments, payroll, contractors, tax remittances, interest, principal, and ending unrestricted cash. Keep restricted processor balances in their own column. Use invoice-level expected payment dates for the largest accounts and historical curves for the long tail. A refund reserve recognized against sales is an accounting estimate; money reserved to fund actual refunds is a liquidity allocation, not a second expense. Maintain an opening reserve plus new provisions less settlements roll-forward and connect each settlement to the originating cohort. Bad-debt expense, contractual credits, and processor chargebacks need separate reason codes because they imply different operating fixes. Under the Base 15-day collection stress, the $77,055 incremental funding requirement would reduce the $135,750 annual cash bridge to $58,695 before other working-capital changes or owner taxes. Annual arithmetic still misses a payroll failure in week three, so inspect the minimum weekly balance. Assign collection ownership before closing, obtain customer remittance instructions through verified channels, and preserve access to historical dispute records. When timing slips, accelerate clean billing, negotiate documented payment plans, and draw only committed facilities permitted by their terms rather than postponing payroll or statutory remittances.

sections.heading: 4. Underwrite trade-claim recoveries without contaminating operating revenue
paragraphs: The mapped play chapter11_trade_claim_convenience_class_rollup purchases documented small trade claims below risk-adjusted expected plan distributions. Treat it as an optional, separately funded investment sleeve, not an assumed revenue stream inside the three acquisition cases. For a $10,000 face claim, suppose a confirmed plan supports a 35% distribution if the claim is allowed, underwriting assigns a 90% probability of that outcome, and the downside outcome pays zero. Expected gross collection is $3,150. Paying $1,800 and reserving $300 for administration produces $1,050 expected economic surplus before financing and taxes. That is a 50% expected return on $2,100 total cash committed, not a 50% annual yield. An eighteen-month wait ties up the purchase price and servicing budget while the operating company still owes payroll. Claim face amount is neither acquired-business sales nor earned fees. Recoveries contain return of invested capital; track basis recovery, economic gain, cash timing, and applicable accounting treatment separately. Do not transfer SBA loan proceeds or restricted operating cash into the sleeve without establishing that the use is permitted under governing program rules and financing documents. If no permitted surplus capital exists, make no claim purchases.

Section 1122(b) of title 11 permits a separate class of sufficiently small unsecured claims when the court approves the amount as reasonable and necessary for administrative convenience. It does not promise a recovery premium to a buyer who splits claims or aggregates holders. Read the actual plan, disclosure statement, confirmation order, class definitions, election terms, and distribution procedures before pricing any convenience treatment. Schedules E/F are sourcing evidence, not a substitute for reconciling the claims register, proofs of claim, amendments, and objections. Inspect purchase orders, delivery evidence, invoices, credits, and payment history to establish the underlying obligation. Section 502 governs allowance and objections; setoff, prior payments, priority disputes, and avoidance exposure can change the economics. For qualifying post-proof transfers other than security transfers, Bankruptcy Rule 3001(e)(2) requires transfer evidence and notice, with a 21-day transferor objection period after mailing unless extended by the court. Follow the rule's applicable branch and local procedures rather than applying one workflow to every instrument. Use PACER and the court-authorized claims agent to verify docket events. Retain assignment authority, seller identity, and payment instructions through independent verification to prevent buying an unsupported or already-transferred claim.

Price the fallback before placing the order. If supported general-unsecured recovery is only 10% of face with the same 90% allowance probability, expected receipts fall to $900 and the $2,100 commitment loses $1,200 before financing costs. If timing extends from eighteen to thirty months, the additional year costs $252 at a simple 12% funding assumption on $2,100. These are separate sensitivities, not independent probabilities to multiply without evidence. Stop affected purchases when the legal or documentary premise fails, enforce documented seller recourse where available, and price only supported general-unsecured recoveries. Recourse is worth less when the seller lacks assets or the contract does not cover the defect. Set debtor-level concentration limits because buying many claims against one estate does not diversify plan risk. Return to the acquisition dashboard each week: collections, labor utilization, customer losses, reversal provision, covenant headroom, and minimum cash. Release a turnaround saving into the forecast only after invoices or payroll verify it. Keep claims distributions outside the canonical operating-sales bridge so an investment windfall cannot conceal customer attrition. Preserve the operating company's ability to serve customers before pursuing delayed recoveries from another company's insolvency.

chapters.question_prompt: How do you allocate startup capital ($30,000–$120,000 USD) and configure a lean, low-opex ($6,000–$25,000 USD/mo) production stack without wasting cash on bloated overhead?
chapters.title: Startup Capital, Lean Infrastructure & Pre-Flight Stack
chapters.subtitle: Reserve-First ETA Capital, SBA and Seller-Note Structures, Twelve Software Layers, and Verified Closing Readiness
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #13, Business Acquisition, ranks #17 with a 86/100 Money-to-Manpower Score: the constraint is capital and operating labor, not software access. This chapter maps seven operator plays: reserve-first capitalization, QoE-led price discipline, SBA and seller-note structuring, aged-entity and tradeline credit discipline, lean infrastructure consolidation, liability isolation, and a cash-led 100-day turnaround. Keep 55% of startup capital in identifiable working-capital reserves, underwrite every financing source, and install only systems that protect collections, payroll, reporting, and customer continuity. Canonical annual owner profits remain $60,000 Conservative, $243,750 Base, and $540,000 Scaled, after interest but before principal repayments. Acquisition funding, business sales, software spending, and owner distributions must remain separate ledgers throughout the six-to-eighteen-month search and transition.

key_metrics.context: Annual acquired-business sales; not purchase consideration

sections.heading: 1. Ring-fence working capital before negotiating the purchase
paragraphs: Play one, reserve-first capitalization, starts with a sources-and-uses schedule that distinguishes buyer cash from purchase price. Allocate 55% of the $30,000–$120,000 startup envelope to working-capital and liquidity reserves before bidding. The three illustrative budgets below sum to $200,000, $600,000, and $1,000,000; they are funding envelopes, not additional scorecard scenarios. Keep reserves in separately identified business accounts or ledger subaccounts, with weekly reporting of unrestricted balances. Security deposits, lender-controlled cash, escrowed purchase consideration, and unavailable credit lines do not count as spendable reserves. The $600,000 envelope commits $330,000 to reserves and only $180,000 to acquisition equity. If the transaction requires $250,000 of buyer equity, raise another $70,000 or change the transaction; do not silently raid payroll liquidity. Reserve coverage against the illustrative monthly overhead bands equals 7.33 months at $110,000 divided by $15,000, 8.25 months at $330,000 divided by $40,000, and 7.86 months at $550,000 divided by $70,000. Those ratios measure overhead coverage, not total survival runway. Inventory purchases, seasonal receivables, taxes, principal payments, and necessary equipment replacement belong in a separate thirteen-week cash forecast. An apparently comfortable cash balance can disappear when annual insurance premiums and the first post-closing payroll fall in the same week.

Play two, QoE-led price discipline, converts diligence from a report purchase into a funding decision. Commission a transaction-sized Quality of Earnings review that bridges tax returns, bank deposits, sales journals, payroll, and monthly management accounts. Require separate schedules for customer concentration, aged receivables, inventory obsolescence, deferred revenue, owner add-backs, and maintenance capital expenditure. A seller claiming $300,000 of adjusted earnings might include a $60,000 owner compensation add-back while the buyer must hire a $90,000 replacement manager. Substituting the actual replacement cost reduces that claimed earnings figure by $90,000, to $210,000, assuming all other adjustments survive verification. Do not add the same owner salary twice or price the business on labor that somebody still must perform. At a negotiated four-times earnings multiple, that correction changes illustrative enterprise value by $360,000. Treat this as transaction math, not a revision to the canonical annual profit cases. Define the working-capital peg using representative monthly balances and seasonality rather than the seller's best month. Document which receivables, inventory, payables, and customer deposits transfer. If source records cannot support collections or normalized earnings, suspend exclusivity spending, narrow the diligence scope, renegotiate consideration, or leave before irreversible closing costs consume the reserve.

Play three, SBA and seller-note structuring, separates acquisition consideration from operating liquidity. An illustrative $1,000,000 purchase could use $180,000 buyer equity, $720,000 senior financing, and a $100,000 seller note; fees and the $330,000 reserve remain separate uses in the $600,000 startup envelope. This capital stack is arithmetic, not a statement that any lender will accept the structure. Obtain written treatment of equity injection, seller standby, subordination, collateral, distributions, and permitted working-capital uses under the applicable program and loan documents. Under 13 CFR 120.150, repayment ability matters; an eligible business still needs credible cash generation. Model payment commencement dates explicitly, especially when a deferred seller note begins amortizing after the transition. Canonical owner profit already includes interest expense, so subtracting interest again understates cash availability. Conversely, principal repayment is excluded and must be deducted before distributions. An illustrative $72,000 annual principal requirement leaves negative $12,000, $171,750, and $468,000 from the Conservative, Base, and Scaled profits, respectively, before incremental capital expenditure, working-capital changes, and owner-level taxes. These are cash bridges, not new profit forecasts. Reject a financing structure that only works by stripping reserves or assuming immediate customer growth; reduce the price, change payment timing, or select a smaller acquisition.

callout.title: Protect the reserve where acquisition budgets usually leak
callout.body: An attractive headline purchase price can conceal expensive working-capital delivery, replacement labor, and payment-timing problems.
items: Require an opening balance-sheet illustration with the letter of intent; identify customer deposits and prepaid obligations before agreeing to the working-capital peg.
Pay diligence providers against named deliverables and staged scopes; release the next tranche only after bank-to-ledger reconciliation supports the seller's revenue.
Negotiate a specific seller transition schedule with hours, introductions, and documentation; avoid paying a vague consulting retainer for availability that never materializes.
Request the lender's complete fee estimate and draft debt schedule early; compare reserve balances after closing, not merely the quoted interest rate.

sections.heading: 2. Install twelve infrastructure layers without buying an enterprise stack
paragraphs: Play five, lean infrastructure consolidation, starts by inventorying the target's working systems before purchasing replacements. Preserve a reliable point-of-sale, dispatch, inventory, or industry billing system through closing unless ownership transfer or security defects make continued use untenable. The twelve-layer matrix supplies explicit USD budgeting inputs, not live vendor quotations: verify prices, feature limits, taxes, renewal terms, and acquisition eligibility before committing. Annual-billed plans can require cash upfront even when the table expresses monthly equivalents. For ten named users and ten managed computers, the listed paid inputs total $443 monthly: Microsoft 365 $60, Bitwarden $40, QuickBooks $38, Gusto $91 for seven employees, Dropbox Sign $15, Make $9, and Backblaze $90. The remaining listed tiers carry zero subscription charges under the stated assumptions. That produces $5,316 in annual recurring subscriptions before taxes, transaction fees, implementation, and specialized operating software. Against the $12,000 infrastructure allowance, $6,684 remains for those additional items. Contractor payment charges, extra CRM seats, backup exclusions, and additional payroll jurisdictions require separate quotes. Do not confuse cheap software with low business overhead: seven employees, insurance, premises, materials, and debt service dominate this model. Each new subscription needs a named owner, export method, cancellation date, and measurable operational purpose.

Configure identity before automation. Use individually assigned Microsoft 365 accounts, multifactor authentication, separate administrative credentials, and a documented recovery contact controlled by the buyer. Store service credentials in Bitwarden collections with role-based access; never inherit the seller's shared mailbox as the permanent administrator account. Microsoft 365 Business Basic does not supply a complete endpoint-management and device-security program, so inventory device protection separately and budget any missing controls. QuickBooks Simple Start is a narrow planning baseline, not a fit for every acquired company: inventory, multiple operational users, consolidated entities, and detailed job costing can justify a different tier or retention of the incumbent ledger. Never share one login to evade seat limits. Keep payroll in Gusto only after verifying state coverage, tax setup, historical balances, benefit deductions, and the closing-date employer arrangement. HubSpot's free tier should serve a small relationship handoff, not a complex sales organization. Export customer and supplier records before changing account ownership. Run a test invoice, a test credit, and a bank reconciliation against controlled sample records. If migration fails, retain the existing system under an explicit transition arrangement and delay the cutover; the buyer needs uninterrupted collections more than a fashionable technology architecture.

Automation belongs behind reconciled source data. Use Airtable for a short transition register, Make for bounded notifications and document routing, and Looker Studio for read-only reporting. Do not let an untested integration create supplier payments or change bank instructions. At an assumed 400 workflow runs per month using twenty billable credits each, an 8,000-credit workload fits the matrix's 10,000-credit planning tier with a 2,000-credit buffer; validate actual vendor metering because connector actions can consume different amounts. Route failures to a named operator and retain a manual checklist that works without the integration. Backblaze workstation backup protects supported local files, not automatically every cloud mailbox or database; inventory each data source and test its separate export or backup path. Cloudflare DNS access must transfer with the domain registrar account, recovery methods, and billing ownership. Reduce duplicate subscriptions only after confirming retention and export requirements. For twelve users, twelve computers, and eight payroll employees, the same pricing inputs total $487 monthly, assuming unchanged tiers elsewhere. The modest $44 increase illustrates why software seat optimization cannot rescue weak acquisition economics. Review the stack after thirty days of actual transaction volumes, then upgrade the specific bottleneck rather than purchasing a bundled suite to anticipate hypothetical complexity.

sections.heading: 3. Underwrite credit honestly and isolate inherited liabilities
paragraphs: Play four is aged_shelf_corp_tradeline_credit_stacking, the TRACK_1 aged-entity and tradeline credit discipline play. Compare a reinstated entity with a newly formed acquisition vehicle on documented liabilities, ownership, filings, banking acceptance, and actual financing terms; entity age is not operating history. A ten-year-old dormant corporation does not have ten years of revenue, and purchased tradelines do not establish repayment capacity. Never attribute the seller's operating record to a separate borrower without accurately explaining the transaction and supplying lender-requested evidence. Verify reinstatement costs, tax arrears, judgments, prior guarantees, and liens before placing capital into an old entity. Promotional credit requires equally plain arithmetic. A hypothetical $50,000 facility with a twelve-month zero-interest promotion and a 3% upfront fee costs $1,500 before other charges. Retiring principal within twelve months requires $4,166.67 monthly, with the final payment adjusted for rounding. Confirm whether the promotion covers purchases, transfers, or cash advances and whether guarantees, utilization changes, or missed payments alter the terms. If $20,000 remains afterward at an illustrative 24% APR, simple first-month interest is about $400 before issuer-specific daily calculations. Halt applications when disclosures or repayment capacity fail; correct the record, use a transparent term facility, or reduce financed spending rather than opening more accounts.

Play six, liability isolation, begins with transaction structure rather than an entity filing receipt. An asset purchase can define assumed obligations, but statutory successor exposure, liens, tax claims, and contract restrictions still require investigation. An equity purchase generally leaves the target's obligations inside the acquired entity. Maintain separate operating accounts, books, contracts, and documented intercompany transfers where multiple entities are justified; extra companies without operational purpose add fees and reconciliation risk. Bank onboarding requires accurate entity and authorized-person information under the bank's customer identification procedures, including the framework in 31 CFR 1020.220. Confirm legal names and payment instructions through independently obtained contact channels before wiring closing funds. Search applicable state UCC records under the debtor's exact legal name, obtain payoff letters, and coordinate lien releases. UCC 9-315 explains why a security interest can continue in collateral after disposition unless the applicable exception or secured-party authorization applies. A database search alone does not establish clean title. Have transaction counsel address state enactments, tax liens, titled assets, and any required clearances. For applicable asset acquisitions, reconcile the purchase-price allocation under 26 U.S.C. 1060 and the parties' Form 8594 reporting. If evidence remains incomplete, change closing deliverables or escrow arrangements rather than treating a seller's verbal assurance as a release.

Insurance and employment hygiene protect the same reserve as credit discipline. Obtain bindable quotes before finalizing the capital budget, with the correct legal entity, operations, locations, payroll, vehicles, and revenue estimates. Compare general liability, property, workers' compensation, cyber, professional liability where relevant, and business interruption against the actual operating exposures. Claims-made policies need particular attention to retroactive dates, prior acts, and extended reporting options; a new policy may not cover earlier events. An illustrative $12,000 annual premium paid upfront consumes $12,000 of cash immediately even though management reporting recognizes $1,000 monthly. Record that timing difference in the cash forecast. Verify license transferability directly with the issuing authority, including ownership-change requirements for regulated trades and locations. Review employee classification, accrued leave, benefit obligations, wage claims, and payroll tax balances without assuming the seller's labels are correct. Under 8 CFR 274a.2, choose and document the applicable Form I-9 approach for continuing acquired employees; retaining predecessor records carries responsibility for their defects. Separate employees from genuine contractors based on the applicable legal tests, not the desired headcount. If coverage, licenses, or payroll setup cannot support uninterrupted operations, arrange a lawful documented transition or defer the affected activity instead of spending reserves to improvise after closing.

sections.heading: 4. Prove the cash bridge and launch a controlled 100-day turnaround
paragraphs: Play seven, a cash-led 100-day turnaround, starts before closing with a rehearsal rather than a transformation announcement. Build an opening cash forecast from bank balances, collectible receivables, supplier terms, payroll dates, taxes, debt schedules, and committed capital expenditure. Assign every input an owner and refresh the forecast weekly. The canonical business economics remain $750,000 sales less $690,000 expenses for $60,000 profit, $1,875,000 less $1,631,250 for $243,750, and $3,000,000 less $2,460,000 for $540,000. These expense totals include interest and exclude principal repayment. For planning, allocate $15,000, $40,000, and $70,000 monthly to a defined recurring overhead subset, respectively. Annualized, those amounts equal $180,000, $480,000, and $840,000, leaving $510,000, $1,151,250, and $1,620,000 of other scorecard expenses. Those residuals cover costs outside the selected overhead subset; they are not spare cash. Define the account mapping explicitly so labor, premises, software, and interest cannot be counted twice. The monthly range is therefore not a claim that the entire acquired company operates on that amount. If a target's actual cost structure cannot fit these definitions without hiding expenses, display the variance and re-underwrite the transaction rather than changing the canonical profit labels.

Stress the cash forecast using customer behavior rather than a uniform percentage reduction applied to profit. At Base sales of $1,875,000 annually, average monthly revenue is $156,250. An additional fifteen days of collections delay ties up approximately $78,125 when using a thirty-day month and assuming evenly distributed credit sales. That consumes 23.67% of the $330,000 reserve without changing recognized revenue or necessarily changing earnings. A customer representing 20% of Base sales accounts for $375,000 annually; losing that account reduces profit by the lost contribution after avoidable costs, not automatically by $375,000 or by 13% of that amount. Obtain customer-level gross contribution evidence before assigning a downside profit figure. Also test a supplier moving from thirty-day terms to payment before shipment, an equipment failure, and the first scheduled seller-note payment. Set intervention triggers in cash terms, such as forecast unrestricted cash falling below the next two payrolls plus committed tax and debt payments. Responses should have identified owners: accelerate undisputed collections, postpone discretionary projects, negotiate documented supplier terms, or draw an already authorized facility within its covenants. Do not count unapproved credit applications or hoped-for owner contributions as available liquidity. Re-run the forecast after each material customer or supplier change.

Before releasing closing funds, require evidence that the buyer can collect money, pay people, access essential systems, and satisfy transaction conditions on the first operating day. The readiness matrix below names artifacts rather than ceremonial meetings. Rehearse payment approvals with a harmless test transaction where permitted, restore a selected backup, validate invoice routing, and walk through payroll calculations without accidentally submitting duplicate wages. Retain written owner assignments for banking, accounting, customer retention, personnel, and technology. Conservative and Base staffing remain seven full-time employees plus three contractors; Scaled remains eight plus four, or twelve people. Do not present external advisers as an invisible operating workforce when recurring work belongs in the cost base. During days one through thirty, stabilize billing and customer relationships; during days thirty-one through sixty, correct reporting and purchasing leakage; during days sixty-one through one hundred, pursue measured pricing and process changes. Keep the original cash forecast alongside actual results so favorable timing cannot masquerade as operating improvement. If opening balances, licenses, insurance, or debt conditions remain unresolved, escalate to the responsible transaction professional and delay the affected commitment. The completion standard is an evidenced operating capability with funded liquidity, not a collection of signed software contracts or an ambitious integration calendar.

chapters.question_prompt: What kills 80% of newcomers in business acquisition, and what forensic metrics detect margin leaks, regulatory landmines, or platform bans before they wipe out capital?
chapters.title: Beginner Traps, Clawbacks & Asymmetric Failure Modes
chapters.subtitle: QoE Forensics, SBA Debt-Service Bridges, UCC Lien Releases, Merchant Reserves & FERC Queue Option Risk
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #13, Business Acquisition, ranks #17 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 86/100: capital and labor intensity punish weak diligence. Canonical annual owner profits are $60,000 Conservative, $243,750 Base, and $540,000 Scaled, after interest but before principal repayments. The question's 80% framing is not an established failure statistic; this chapter replaces it with measurable loss mechanisms. Seven mapped operating plays organize the defense: QoE normalization, working-capital protection, debt-service structuring, customer retention, liability containment, payment-platform continuity, and powered-land option screening. Each connects evidence to unit economics, escalation thresholds, and a practical fallback. The objective is to reject fragile earnings, contain inherited obligations, and preserve operating liquidity before a lender, customer, regulator, or processor forces the decision.
