Cash check: preserve the canonical profit basis, model principal separately, and test actual lender covenants and working-capital needs before fixing purchase terms.

sections.heading: 4. Convert diligence evidence into a bounded 100-day operating system
paragraphs: At signing, convert unresolved diligence findings into a transition register rather than leaving them inside a report. Every item needs an operating consequence, accountable person, due date, supporting artifact, and escalation threshold. A customer concentration finding becomes a retention conversation owned by the operating manager; a covenant becomes a scheduled calculation owned by the controller; a permit condition becomes an agency-confirmed task reviewed by counsel. During days 1–30, stabilize access, cash visibility, payroll, customer communication, and essential vendor payments. During days 31–60, close the first repeatable monthly reporting cycle and resolve inherited account mapping errors. During days 61–100, automate only workflows that already reconcile manually. Do not migrate accounting systems simply because the integration contractor prefers another platform. Require a documented operating benefit and a reversible migration plan. Keep the four delivery employees focused on service continuity, collecting only the operational evidence needed for exception resolution. P7 succeeds when the acquired business keeps customers and produces dependable records, not when the acquisition desk displays the largest collection of dashboards. Preserve the seller's original records through the agreed retention period.

Refresh evidence according to decision exposure. Bank liquidity may need daily review, accounting exceptions weekly review, and formal ledger reconciliations monthly review. Use lender reporting deadlines and license renewal dates rather than an arbitrary universal schedule. Repeat lien and litigation searches at counsel-directed transaction milestones; repeatedly downloading annual Census releases adds no information. Record stale-source warnings separately from actual adverse findings. An unavailable portal is a retrieval exception, not evidence that a license expired. Maintain replayable imports and test recovery from a revoked token, corrupted file, changed column name, and interrupted download. Track exception age, unreconciled dollars, connector failures, and customer-retention actions completed, rather than celebrating API-call volume. The controller should be able to reproduce the monthly cash bridge without the contractor being online. Store current runbooks alongside access inventories, backup locations, and credential-rotation responsibilities. Remove departed seller and contractor access promptly while preserving required records. This turns back-office automation into durable operating capacity instead of a fragile dependency on one technically skilled person or a forgotten personal account.

Measure the information edge against the same scorecard throughout ownership. Conservative and Base retain seven full-time employees plus three contractors; Scaled permits eight full-time employees plus four contractors, totaling twelve people. The larger case is a separate operating scenario, not permission to quietly expand the Base pod. Put subscription fees, connector maintenance, specialist retainers, and reporting labor inside the expense model supporting each margin. If those costs were omitted, show the resulting variance rather than claiming that automation preserves the stated profit automatically. Keep the $30,000–$120,000 startup-capital range distinct from annual sales, owner profit, and borrowed acquisition principal. Evaluate tools by fewer unresolved liabilities, faster reconciled closes, earlier attrition detection, and better-supported financing decisions. None of those benefits creates revenue until the operating business actually earns recognized sales. Review the seven plays quarterly and retire datasets that no longer change a decision. The desk's advantage is a short, defensible path from source evidence to action, maintained within the team's real capacity and the debt structure's actual cash demands.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #13, Business Acquisition, ranks #17 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 86/100: capital and labor intensity make transaction discipline essential. This chapter maps seven operator plays: targeted sourcing, mandate qualification, QoE, debt structuring, contract-and-license diligence, closing transition, and 100-day retention. A seven-full-time, three-contractor pod must distinguish buying its own operating business from arranging securities transactions for others. Build the purchase agreement around collectible remedies, assignable customer contracts, funded working capital, and licenses effective at transfer. Canonical annual owner profits are $60,000 Conservative, $243,750 Base, and $540,000 Scaled, after interest but before principal repayments. Use documented outreach, state-specific successor-tax checks, lender-approved debt terms, and evidence-backed closing conditions to keep those operating cases separate from acquisition funding.

sections.heading: 1. Separate principal acquisitions from regulated intermediary activity
paragraphs: Organize Candidate #13 around seven plays with named deliverables: targeted sourcing produces a seller list; mandate qualification establishes buyer capacity and seller authority; QoE establishes maintainable earnings; debt structuring establishes funded terms; contract-and-license diligence establishes transferable operating rights; closing transition establishes ownership and access; 100-day retention protects customers and employees. These are this chapter's operating map, not seven separate revenue streams. Use seven full-time roles: owner/general manager, finance lead, operations lead, sales lead, and three delivery employees. Reserve three contractor slots for transaction counsel, a QoE/tax accountant, and a systems-integration specialist. The owner owns the transaction decision; specialists produce evidence rather than silently inheriting authority. At Scaled, add one service lead and one sector specialist, reaching eight employees and four contractors. Keep one live exclusivity process within the smaller pod unless another deal can be staffed without borrowing delivery capacity. Record each workstream, decision owner, document dependency, and statutory deadline in Airtable or a controlled spreadsheet. A beautifully populated data room does not establish that a contractor's license transfers, a customer accepts assignment, or a seller actually owns the shares being sold. Those conclusions require specific evidence.

The principal-versus-intermediary distinction comes before any fee discussion. Buying an operating company for your own account differs from soliciting investors or arranging another party's securities transaction for compensation. Exchange Act Section 15(a), 15 U.S.C. 78o(a), supplies the federal broker-registration starting point; the M&A broker exemption in Section 15(b)(13) is conditional, not a blanket permission for success fees. Counsel must test the eligible privately held company definition, applicable size thresholds, buyer control and active management, required disclosures, and every excluded activity. Custody of transaction funds, public offerings, passive-buyer transactions, and certain financing or buyer-group activities can defeat reliance. Verify current threshold adjustments rather than copying an old broker presentation. State securities registration and exemption analysis remains separate, and associated real estate can introduce real-estate licensing requirements. In California, Business and Professions Code Section 10131(a) reaches compensated brokerage of business opportunities as well as real estate. Do not assume a federal securities exemption answers that question. For mandate qualification, document whether the pod acts as principal, adviser, referral source, or intermediary, and who pays whom. Calling compensation a consulting fee does not change the activities performed or resolve a registration problem.

Build a jurisdiction register using actual operating locations, employee locations, customer services, regulated assets, and deal structure. An asset purchase can require fresh permits, tax registrations, assumed-name filings, and contract assignments; an equity purchase preserves the entity but may trigger ownership-change notifications or approvals. Federal antitrust law also applies below premerger reporting thresholds: screen competitive overlap under Clayton Act Section 7 and separately test current Hart-Scott-Rodino filing rules when transaction size or aggregation warrants it. SBA eligibility is another distinct analysis, not a substitute for licensing. Have the lender identify the current SBA SOP 50 10 edition, ownership-change rules, equity injection evidence, guarantees, seller debt treatment, and required operating permits in writing. A restaurant's liquor permit, a contractor's qualifying individual, and a healthcare provider's enrollment each require their own authority-specific review. The operations lead should ask the issuing agency whether the planned structure allows uninterrupted service and obtain a written answer or recorded official instruction. If permission cannot be effective at closing, redesign timing or exclude the affected activity. Never solve a licensing gap by borrowing the seller's credentials informally while the buyer operates under a different entity.

Reserve the three contractor slots explicitly and maintain one shared exception register so transaction work does not consume the delivery team's week.

sections.heading: 2. Turn diligence findings into funded, collectible contract rights
paragraphs: For the QoE and contract-and-license plays, draft the purchase agreement from a linked exception register rather than recycling a clean template. Define purchased assets, excluded assets, assumed liabilities, excluded liabilities, transferred contracts, inventory standards, cash treatment, and debt-like items separately. Equity transactions require equivalent clarity about capitalization, subsidiaries, leakage, and liabilities remaining inside the acquired entity. State the working-capital peg, reference accounting policies, sample calculation, delivery dates, objection procedure, and independent accountant's limited role. Otherwise, the seller can win the price negotiation again through closing-account classifications. Tie representations to schedules covering taxes, employment, permits, litigation, cybersecurity, material customers, intellectual property, and related-party arrangements. Require identified customer consents and specified lien releases as closing conditions, not optimistic post-closing tasks. Specify indemnity baskets, caps, survival periods, escrow release dates, notice requirements, and who controls third-party claims. Separate known tax or wage exposures into negotiated special indemnities with realistic security. A broad promise from an empty seller entity is weaker than a narrow remedy backed by retained cash. Counsel should align fraud treatment and exclusive-remedy language with governing law rather than assuming one state's drafting conventions travel unchanged to every deal.

The adviser and sourcing agreements need their own commercial architecture. Scope should identify permitted services, deliverables, excluded authority, confidentiality duties, and the buyer's right to stop work. A fee trigger must say whether compensation arises on signing, funded closing, or receipt of specified consideration; define earnouts, rollover equity, assumed debt, installment payments, and broken transactions explicitly. For a closing-based fee, include a worked calculation and prohibit duplicate claims for the same introduction. Use a narrowly drafted anti-circumvention provision tied to named counterparties, documented introductions, preexisting-contact exclusions, and a defined tail. It should not become an indefinite tax on unrelated acquisitions. A liability cap should identify covered losses and negotiated exceptions, while acknowledging that applicable law can restrict exclusions. Specify governing law, forum or arbitration rules, emergency relief, notice addresses, and treatment of collection costs. IP/data ownership should distinguish buyer-owned work product, preexisting adviser tools, licensed deliverables, and source records supplied by the target. Limit subcontractor access and require return or controlled deletion at termination. Finally, make compensation conditional on lawful performance; a contract cannot manufacture an exemption from broker-registration requirements that the actual services fail to satisfy.

Translate hidden liabilities into a tax, employment, and secured-creditor closing schedule. For applicable asset acquisitions, Internal Revenue Code Section 1060 and Form 8594 require purchase-price allocation reporting; coordinate buyer and seller positions, contingent consideration, and later adjustments. Do not assume the parties can simply label all value goodwill to produce their preferred tax result. State successor-tax procedures require jurisdiction-specific action: California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 6811 addresses purchase-price withholding for certain business sales, while New York Tax Law Section 1141(c) imposes advance bulk-sale notification procedures. Employment diligence should reconcile payroll registers, time records, contractor classifications, accrued leave, benefit plans, and pending claims. Apply FLSA recordkeeping and wage rules, state wage-payment requirements, and structure-specific successor principles; excluded-liability language alone does not settle employee or government claims. Seven employees do not automatically trigger federal WARN, but analyze the actual employer, aggregated operations, transaction timing, and state mini-WARN rules. Search UCC records in the proper debtor jurisdiction, confirm exact legal names, and obtain payoff letters with release mechanics. Also search relevant tax liens and titled assets; a clean UCC search does not establish clean title to everything.

sections.heading: 3. Run honest sourcing and discovery without leaking target information
paragraphs: Targeted sourcing should start with a manually reviewed business list, documented source, relevant industry thesis, and one accountable sales lead. Do not assume every acquisition inquiry is a commercial advertisement or every business recipient falls outside outreach rules; classify the message and channel before launching a sequence. For commercial email covered by CAN-SPAM, 15 U.S.C. 7704 requires accurate routing information, nondeceptive subjects, required sender information and advertising identification where applicable, a valid postal address, and a functioning opt-out. Honor covered opt-outs within ten business days and prevent contractors from reimporting suppressed contacts. Use a cautious first-touch script: 'Subject: Ownership discussion about your business. I am the principal of an acquisition company evaluating established businesses in your sector. Your service mix appears relevant to our search. Would you consider a private conversation about ownership succession? We have not reviewed your financials or obtained financing approval for your company. Reply stop and we will end acquisition outreach.' Append the sender's actual legal identity, required identification, and postal address before sending. Never describe a purchased contact list as a personal referral or imply that an SBA lender has already approved an unnamed target.

For phone outreach, separate live manual calls from prerecorded messages, artificial voices, automated dialing, and texts. TCPA restrictions under 47 U.S.C. 227 and 47 CFR 64.1200 depend on technology, number type, purpose, and consent; state telephone-solicitation and recording rules can add obligations. A published business number is not universal permission for automated campaigns, and an owner may publish a mobile number. Check applicable calling-hour and suppression requirements before contact, retain the basis for any consent, and avoid recording until the applicable authorization is established. Use this live-call opening: 'Hello, I am calling as a potential buyer, not on behalf of your lender or a government agency. Is this a reasonable time for a brief ownership-succession question? If you prefer no further calls, I will record that immediately.' For an intermediary, say: 'Before exchanging targets, please identify your client, authority, licensing or exemption basis, and proposed fee trigger. We will agree scope in writing before introductions.' Log the answer without turning it into a legal conclusion. The sales lead owns suppression records; counsel resolves channel uncertainty before the systems contractor activates HubSpot or another sequence engine.

Discovery begins with authority and information rights, not a request for the entire customer database. Use this seller script: 'Who owns the equity or assets, who can authorize this discussion, and which other approvals are required? What customer, landlord, lender, or license conditions could change on transfer? Please start with redacted monthly statements and a revenue-concentration summary; we will define deeper access under a confidentiality agreement.' Then ask: 'Which earnings adjustments represent costs a replacement operator will actually avoid, and what evidence supports each adjustment?' For employees, ask about roles and retention risks before demanding individual medical or identity documents. Stage access in SharePoint or another controlled data room with named users, expiration dates, and download logs. Where buyer and target compete, counsel should design clean-team restrictions for pricing, customer-level margins, and forward strategy. An NDA does not authorize premature operational control or unrestricted competitive information exchange. Assess whether California privacy requirements or sector rules cover the target and its disclosures; an acquisition-related transfer provision is not permission for unrelated marketing reuse. Keep live credentials, payment-card data, and unnecessary personal identifiers out of routine diligence. Contract for deletion or restricted retention if the transaction ends.

sections.heading: 4. Reconcile lender covenants, closing cash, and the first 100 days
paragraphs: Debt structuring must preserve the scorecard's accounting boundary. Conservative acquired-business sales of $750,000 at 8% produce $60,000 annual owner net profit; Base sales of $1,875,000 at 13.0% produce $243,750; Scaled sales of $3,000,000 at 18% produce $540,000. These margins are after interest and before principal repayments. Purchase price, loan proceeds, seller-note principal, and customer transaction volume are not additional recognized operating revenue. Show principal service on a separate cash bridge, alongside capital expenditure and working-capital changes, without silently changing the canonical profit cases. As an illustrative bridge only, $100,000 of annual principal payments would leave $143,750 from Base profit before additional cash uses; that principal amount is an assumption, not a scorecard input. Build lender coverage calculations from the lender's defined numerator, denominator, testing period, and permitted adjustments rather than treating net margin as debt-service coverage. Review restrictions on distributions, additional debt, liens, acquisitions, ownership changes, and seller-note payments. Keep the $30,000–$120,000 startup-capital range distinct from the $6,000–$25,000 monthly operating-expense planning range; neither range independently proves that a particular purchase price or leverage package works. Use actual target statements and funded terms to establish affordability.

The closing-transition play needs a single funds-flow document connecting the signed agreement, lender instructions, escrow ledger, payoff letters, and post-closing liquidity. Authenticate wire instructions through a known telephone number obtained independently of the payment email; require two-person review and preserve the verification record. Finance should reconcile every dollar to buyer equity, acquisition debt, seller consideration, tax withholding, transaction expenses, and retained working cash. Counsel checks that release obligations cover the assets actually purchased and that recording or filing responsibilities have named owners. The operations lead verifies insurance inception, bank-signing authority, merchant-account arrangements, payroll readiness, and customer-contract consents. Do not assume payment-processing accounts or software subscriptions transfer merely because equipment and goodwill do. For employment onboarding, determine the applicable Form I-9 treatment and document whether the buyer adopts qualifying predecessor records or completes new verification under the relevant successor rules. Review benefit continuity, COBRA obligations where applicable, and accrued-pay treatment with the accounting contractor and counsel. A small buyer can inherit complexity from a larger seller's benefit arrangements. Release funds only under the agreed escrow instructions after required evidence is complete; do not use an informal promise to repair essential operating authority after money moves.

During the 100-day retention play, maintain the contractual and statutory evidence as operating controls rather than archiving everything at closing. The finance lead owns a covenant calendar, tax deadlines, indemnity notice dates, working-capital objection periods, and seller-note restrictions. Operations owns permit renewals, qualifying-person continuity, wage controls, and employee transition commitments. Sales tracks customer contacts, required consents, churn signals, and service promises made during diligence. Use QuickBooks or the target's existing ledger for financial reporting, with controlled exports into a weekly cash forecast; automate reminders and reconciliations before automating unusual judgment calls. Hold weekly exception reviews for thirty days, then biweekly through day one hundred, while contractual deadlines remain individually tracked. Compare retained customer gross profit and actual staffing costs against QoE assumptions instead of celebrating signed revenue alone. Route an undisclosed tax claim or threatened customer termination immediately to the responsible specialist so notice periods do not expire. The seven-employee, three-contractor pod cannot absorb unlimited integration projects: prioritize payroll, collections, licenses, service continuity, and cash visibility. Defer cosmetic system migrations until those controls stabilize. Expand toward eight employees and four contractors only when the Scaled case supports the additional capacity and lenders permit the resulting commitments.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #13, Business Acquisition, ranks #17 with a 86/100 Money-to-Manpower Score: automation improves operating discipline, but does not remove capital intensity or leverage. This chapter maps seven plays: sourcing research, qualification, QoE evidence preparation, financial reporting, back-office routing, fulfillment coordination, and distribution feedback. A 2 FT + 2 C pod uses Python, authenticated webhooks, bounded language-model tasks, and human release decisions to target 70%+ automation of measured repetitive work. Canonical annual owner profit remains $60,000 Conservative, $243,750 Base, and $540,000 Scaled, after interest and before principal repayments. The Scaled case requires 3 FT + 3 C. Build durable evidence trails, price every completed workflow, and convert verified customer outcomes into repeatable acquisition channels without confusing pipeline value with acquired-business sales.

sections.heading: 1. Map Seven Plays to Accountable People Before Automating Work
paragraphs: Start with the acquisition thesis, not an agent shopping list. Candidate #13 buys and operates cash-flowing SMBs; its revenue is acquired-business sales, not purchase consideration, seller proceeds, or the face value of financing. For this chapter, map the seven operator plays explicitly: sourcing research, qualification, QoE evidence preparation, financial reporting, back-office routing, fulfillment coordination, and distribution feedback. Give every play an input contract, an evidence record, a responsible person, and a reversible output. A broker teaser can become a research record automatically; it cannot become an investment conclusion merely because a model produces fluent prose. Assign the seven full-time seats to the owner and investment lead, general manager, controller, sourcing and growth lead, customer success lead, and two delivery operators. Assign the three contractor seats to transaction counsel, a QoE specialist, and an automation engineer, with their hours budgeted rather than treated as unlimited capacity. This is an illustrative staffing allocation within the canonical four-person constraint, not ten acquisition staff sitting above an uncounted workforce. Choose targets whose delivery model actually fits these seats. If the acquired company needs more field labor, reconcile that requirement before underwriting its operating margin or promising an automated turnaround.

Define the 70%+ objective using observed work, not the number of software features enabled. During ten business days, record eligible repetitive tasks and their manual baseline minutes across all seven plays. Freeze that denominator before the pilot. An illustrative week contains 1,000 eligible task instances consuming 100 manual hours; automation completes 760 instances without correction, but exception handling, sampled QA, and system maintenance still consume 26 hours. The task automation rate is 76%, while net repetitive labor displacement is 74%; report both and also report all operating hours outside the eligible pool. Count failed attempts and rework against the result instead of quietly deleting them from the sample. Consequential decisions remain human work even when evidence assembly is automated: purchase offers, lender representations, employee actions, vendor bank changes, customer credits, and public claims require named release authority. Break results out by play because fast teaser extraction can otherwise conceal broken fulfillment routing. The general manager reviews weekly exception volume against actual staff availability. When automation creates more review work than the pod can absorb, reduce intake or narrow the workflow. Do not manufacture a favorable percentage by excluding the hardest ordinary cases after the measurement period has begun.

Sequence implementation around the first 100 operating days. Before closing, use seller-authorized read access and keep diligence files separate from the acquired company's production systems. During days 1 through 30, automate bank-feed reconciliation preparation, daily collections visibility, and customer handoff reminders; these expose hidden liabilities and attrition before growth experiments amplify them. During days 31 through 60, standardize invoice routing, delivery checklists, and renewal alerts. During days 61 through 100, expand sourcing and distribution only after service reliability and cash conversion hold steady. The canonical $30,000–$120,000 startup capital range is acquisition context, not a software budget, and the $6,000–$25,000 monthly opex range is not a complete income statement. Build an explicit bridge for cost of delivery, overhead, interest, and working capital rather than forcing those ranges to equal scenario expenses. The six-to-eighteen-month first-deal horizon also means sourcing automation must survive long quiet periods without inventing urgency. Maintain a target exclusion register for geography, licensing, customer concentration, and incompatible labor requirements. Use the matrix below as ownership design: each output has a release boundary and an observable failure signal, so a departing contractor cannot leave behind an opaque system nobody can safely operate.

callout.title: Protect the Acquisition Thesis From Automated Optimism
callout.body: Veteran operators use automation to expose disagreement early, not to make every target resemble the investment memorandum.
items: Preserve the original seller export and checksum it before normalizing accounts; otherwise a changing chart of accounts can erase the trail behind a QoE adjustment.
Track seller involvement by customer and delivery task during transition; apparent automation savings can actually be unpaid seller labor that disappears after closing.
Build concentration alerts from invoiced and collected revenue separately; a large customer's slow payments can matter before their revenue share changes.
Make the automation engineer document a manual close and dispatch procedure before expanding workflows; contractor availability must not determine whether the business can collect cash.

sections.heading: 2. Build Evidence-Linked Python and Webhook Pipelines With Safe Recovery
paragraphs: Use a narrow Python service as the integration spine, with QuickBooks Online or Xero as the accounting record and HubSpot as the relationship record where those products fit the acquired company. An HTTPS endpoint receives provider events through a managed gateway; implement each provider's documented authentication scheme rather than assuming every webhook uses the same signature format. Verify the raw body before decoding, check timestamps when supported, and reject replayed delivery identifiers. Persist the accepted event before acknowledging it, then process asynchronously. A Python 3.9 worker can use json, decimal, hashlib, hmac, urllib.request, and sqlite3 without third-party packages. SQLite is appropriate for a low-volume single-writer pilot with tested backups; higher concurrency requires a deliberately selected durable queue and database, not additional writers bolted onto a fragile local file. Store provider, tenant, event identifier, payload digest, received time, schema version, attempt count, and processing state. Fetch authoritative records using least-privilege credentials where the webhook contains only an identifier. Validate currency, dates, required fields, and tenant ownership before creating internal tasks. A malformed invoice must enter an exception queue instead of becoming a zero-dollar transaction that silently improves the dashboard. Keep sensitive payloads out of routine application logs.

Insert language models only where probabilistic interpretation is useful: classifying seller documents, extracting contract renewal terms, drafting customer follow-ups, and summarizing reconciliation exceptions. Treat every uploaded document as untrusted content, including text that tells the model to reveal secrets or contact outside services. The extraction prompt requires a bounded JSON object with source page, quoted evidence, proposed value, and an explicit unresolved state for missing evidence. Python validates the schema and checks that quoted text actually appears in the supplied source. Confidence scores may prioritize review, but cannot prove a revenue recognition judgment or establish that an add-back is recurring. Keep payment credentials and unrestricted network tools outside the model context. Use decimal.Decimal for amounts and deterministic reconciliation rules for totals; a model does not calculate the final purchase-price bridge. Compare monthly sales across the general ledger, invoice register, bank deposits, credit notes, and tax records, explaining timing differences rather than forcing equality. The QoE contractor signs off disputed adjustments and the controller owns posting decisions. Restrict seller data to authorized users and service providers, minimize what leaves the document repository, and set retention by transaction need, contractual obligations, and applicable recordkeeping requirements.

Design every external write for interruption. A workflow state machine should distinguish received, validated, drafted, reviewed, released, and reconciled records, with failed events held separately for investigation. Persist a stable operation key before sending an invoice draft or CRM update. Where the destination supports idempotency keys, use them; otherwise query the destination by your external reference before replaying an uncertain request. A timeout after transmission does not prove the write failed. Retry transient rate limits and server errors with bounded exponential backoff and jitter, honoring provider retry instructions, but route authorization failures and invalid schemas to a person. After three unsuccessful attempts in this illustrative policy, move the event into a dead-letter queue with an owner and response deadline. Reconcile event counts against source-system exports each day because webhook delivery alone does not establish completeness. When a provider fails, the customer success lead uses the last validated dispatch list and the controller prepares payments through the existing bank workflow. Import the resulting manual references before restarting automation. Test restoration from backup, duplicate event delivery, delayed messages, and partial posting in a sandbox. Release a connector only after the operator can demonstrate recovery without duplicate customer charges or lost fulfillment commitments.

sections.heading: 3. Price Automated Runs and Reconcile Them to Owner Cash
paragraphs: Keep the three scorecard scenarios fixed while evaluating automation underneath them. Conservative sales of $750,000 at 8% produce $60,000 annual owner net profit; Base sales of $1,875,000 at 13.0% produce $243,750; Scaled sales of $3,000,000 at 18% produce $540,000. The corresponding expense envelopes are $690,000, $1,631,250, and $2,460,000, respectively. These margins include interest and precede principal repayments. Do not add estimated automation savings to those profits unless rebuilding the entire scenario with an explicit expense bridge. Conservative and Base both use 2 FT + 2 C, while Scaled uses 8 FT + 4 C, or twelve people. A software demonstration cannot justify calling the Scaled case a four-person operation. Principal belongs in a separate cash schedule: an illustrative $90,000 annual principal requirement would leave Base profit less principal of $153,750, before working-capital movements, capital expenditures, and owner-level taxes. That amount is neither revised scorecard profit nor automatically distributable cash. Read the executed loan documents for reporting dates, debt-service definitions, restricted payments, and permitted indebtedness. SBA program eligibility and use-of-proceeds requirements remain relevant when structuring an acquisition; automated summaries cannot replace lender confirmation of the actual financing terms, seller-note treatment, and current program requirements.

Price one workflow with a transparent bill of materials. Assume an evidence-preparation run uses 12,000 input tokens at an illustrative $3 per million and 2,000 output tokens at an illustrative $15 per million, producing $0.066 of model cost. Add $0.014 for queue, storage, and request handling, giving $0.080 before retries and review. These are planning rates, not a vendor quotation. If 10% of runs require one complete additional attempt, expected machine cost is $0.088 per original run. If 20% require three minutes of human review at a loaded $45 hourly rate, expected review cost is $0.450, making variable cost $0.538 per run. At 2,000 original runs monthly, variable cost is $1,076. Add $600 for connector subscriptions and maintenance allocation to reach $1,676 monthly, or $0.838 per completed run when all original runs eventually complete. Failed terminal runs reduce that denominator and increase effective unit cost. Separate cash invoices from allocated employee time so the accounting expense bridge does not count the same salary twice. Log actual tokens, retries, review minutes, completion outcomes, and maintenance effort by play. A cheap extraction step can still create an expensive workflow when ambiguous documents repeatedly consume specialist attention downstream.

Translate labor capacity into economics without pretending that saved minutes immediately become cash. If the same illustrative workload previously required four minutes per run at $45 per hour, its loaded labor value was $6,000 monthly. Subtracting the $1,676 workflow cost yields $4,324 of potential capacity value, not automatic incremental profit. The four-person pod may redeploy that time into collections, customer retention, and delivery quality while payroll remains unchanged. Recognize a cash saving only when a real expense disappears, such as a reduced contractor invoice or an avoided incremental hire supported by capacity records. Monitor review precision, correction rates, and cash outcomes together. One erroneous supplier payment can overwhelm months of token savings; independently verify bank changes using a previously trusted contact channel and keep payment release separate from invoice extraction. Maintain payroll records required by 29 CFR 516.2 and tax records under 26 U.S.C. 6001 even when document handling becomes automated. For hidden-liability monitoring, compare vendor statements, aged payables, payroll accruals, and customer deposits against the opening balance sheet. Escalate discrepancies to the controller and transaction counsel before treating them as post-close operating expenses. Review automation economics monthly alongside attrition and debt service, because efficiency that damages revenue or obscures liabilities does not improve acquisition quality.

callout.title: Verify Four Conditions Before Expanding Automation
callout.body: The general manager records these checks for each material workflow change; automation volume expands only within demonstrated review and recovery capacity.

sections.heading: 4. Turn Verified Operating Outcomes Into Distribution Flywheels
paragraphs: Separate acquisition sourcing from customer demand generation in both the CRM and the income statement. The sourcing loop begins with thesis-matched businesses, advances through permissioned research and human qualification, and ends with a signed transaction only when diligence and financing support it. The operating-company growth loop begins with a real customer need and ends with delivered, recognized sales and measured collections. Build programmatic pages only from verified service coverage, actual capabilities, and useful operating data. A regional maintenance business might publish genuine service-area pages showing response windows and equipment supported; it should not generate hundreds of near-identical pages for locations it cannot serve. Use Search Console for search performance, HubSpot for lead stages, and the accounting ledger for recognized revenue. Assign campaign identifiers at inquiry creation and retain them through quote, job, invoice, and collection. The growth lead reviews factual claims while a delivery operator confirms capacity before publication. Treat model-written pages as drafts and prevent customer records from leaking into public examples. Feed lost-quote reasons back into service design and qualification, not merely into another batch of content. This connects play seven to plays two and six without mistaking website traffic or the seller pipeline's estimated value for operator revenue.

Create a referral loop from completed work rather than manufactured enthusiasm. After the customer success lead verifies delivery and resolves open complaints, send a concise request for an introduction or an honest review. Do not condition incentives on positive sentiment, fabricate testimonials, or ask a model to impersonate a customer; 16 CFR Part 465 addresses deceptive review and testimonial practices. Obtain permission before naming a customer or publishing their results. A useful viral asset is a shareable maintenance checklist or operating benchmark derived from authorized, sufficiently aggregated records, with a clear path back to an actual service offering. For outbound acquisition sourcing, prepare a small list of thesis-matched owners from permitted sources and have the investment lead approve individualized messages. Commercial email must meet applicable 15 U.S.C. 7704 requirements, including accurate routing information, truthful subject lines, required identification, a valid postal address, and functioning opt-out handling. Process opt-outs within ten business days and suppress future sends across connected systems. Keep telephone and text campaigns outside this email workflow until their separate rules and permissions are assessed. Track reply quality and seller trust, not just delivery volume. An automated message that misstates the buyer's capital availability can damage both sourcing relationships and later transaction disclosures.

Run the flywheel as a cohort experiment with operational stop rules. For an illustrative customer campaign, $2,400 of fully identified acquisition spending produces 40 qualified inquiries and eight new customers, giving $300 acquisition cost per customer. If those customers produce $12,000 in collected sales and $4,800 in contribution before acquisition spending, the cohort leaves $2,400 after acquisition spending and before overhead, interest, and other unallocated expenses. These are channel diagnostics, not an additional scorecard scenario or permission to add $2,400 to canonical owner profit. Avoid counting an existing customer's routine purchase as newly acquired revenue merely because they clicked an email. Review cohorts by first purchase month, source, repeat purchases, refunds, and service load. Pause a channel when cancellations, overdue receivables, or delivery backlog exceed the thresholds set by the general manager before launch. Return those failure reasons to qualification rules and fulfillment planning, creating a feedback loop grounded in business outcomes. On the acquisition side, measure research-to-conversation and conversation-to-qualified-opportunity rates separately, retaining rejection reasons for the next sourcing cycle. Publish one weekly operating packet covering cash, customer retention, exceptions, automation cost, and channel cohorts. Scale only the loops whose evidence survives reconciliation and whose review burden fits the people actually on payroll and contract.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #13, Business Acquisition, ranks #17 with a 86/100 Money-to-Manpower Score: returns depend on disciplined ownership, not invisible labor. This chapter maps seven operator plays: acquisition screening, quality of earnings, capital structuring, 100-day integration, customer retention, reporting automation, and exit readiness. Assign those plays across seven full-time seats and three contractors before expanding to eight full-time seats and four contractors. Canonical annual owner profits are $60,000 Conservative, $243,750 Base, and $540,000 Scaled, after interest but before principal repayments. Weekly evidence-backed scorecards, customer and operating-counterparty concentration limits of 25%, signed IP transfers, and clean accrual cohorts make performance transferable. Value the resulting earnings only after replacing owner labor, testing cash conversion, and subtracting debt from enterprise value.

sections.heading: 1. Assign seven plays to seven employees without hiding owner labor
paragraphs: Start with seats, decision rights, and recurring deliverables rather than a miniature private-equity organization chart. Candidate #13 supports seven full-time employees and three contractors in both Conservative and Base cases; the working owner occupies one of those seven seats. Use this chapter's seven-play mapping consistently: acquisition screening, quality of earnings, capital structuring, 100-day integration, customer retention, reporting automation, and exit readiness. The owner leads screening and capital structuring; the controller leads quality of earnings and reporting; the operations lead runs integration; the customer lead owns retention; and the owner coordinates exit readiness through records maintained by every seat. Sales and delivery employees execute these plays without becoming additional department heads. Give each critical process one accountable employee, one trained backup, and one measurable output. A responsibility shared by everybody usually becomes an unresolved seller dependency. During diligence, compare this roster with actual payroll, overtime, seasonality, seller hours, and outsourced work. A business requiring eleven permanent employees does not fit this pod simply because its historical payroll labels several workers as vendors. Price the actual staffing requirement before signing, and reject economics that depend on the seller continuing unpaid.

The first full-time seat is the owner-general manager, responsible for cash allocation, lender communication, pricing exceptions, and succession. The second is an operations lead who controls scheduling, capacity, safety procedures, and acceptance standards. The third is a controller who owns accrual close, payroll review, covenant calculations, and the evidence room. The fourth is a customer-success lead responsible for renewals, complaints, and account-level margin. The fifth is a sales and estimating lead who quotes within approved price bands and records acquisition source. Seats six and seven are delivery specialists with complementary technical skills and documented cross-training. Separate vendor creation, payment preparation, and payment release: the bookkeeper prepares, the controller reviews, and the owner releases through bank controls. Nobody should create a supplier and independently approve that supplier's payment. Maintain named backups for bank access and customer escalation without sharing credentials. At Scaled, add an eighth employee for delivery capacity and a fourth contractor for defined overflow work. Promote an existing employee only when their prior workload has a funded replacement; relabeling a technician as manager does not create free capacity. Every recurring hour must land in a seat, contractor scope, or explicit owner workload.

Run the 100-day transition as a transfer of operating control, not an indefinite seller apprenticeship. During days 1–30, capture credential ownership, customer commitments, quoting logic, supplier terms, and seller-only decisions. During days 31–60, require employees to perform those decisions using written tolerances while the seller observes. During days 61–100, test an owner-absence week and close every exception through a named backup. Record seller transition assistance separately from recurring operating capacity, with a finite scope and cost. The canonical Conservative case produces only $60,000 annual owner profit on $750,000 sales, so seven employees are affordable only with a compatible wage structure, delivery model, and nonlabor cost base. The Base case is $1,875,000 sales and $243,750 profit; Scaled is $3,000,000 sales and $540,000 profit. Those figures imply total modeled costs of $690,000, $1,631,250, and $2,460,000 respectively, including interest within the stated profit basis. Test compensation against those totals rather than inserting an additional management layer. Measure productive capacity using completed, accepted jobs per paid hour. Expansion requires sustained contribution after the proposed hire, not merely a fuller sales pipeline. Preserve the exact scenario profits when presenting the scorecard; show any revised staffing economics as a separate acquisition underwriting case.

callout.title: Buy the operating system, not the seller's permanent availability
callout.body: Transferability appears in routine evidence before it appears in a buyer's valuation model. Make these four practices part of the acquisition plan.
items: Reconcile seller calendars against payroll and job logs; price recurring seller labor before accepting discretionary earnings adjustments.
Ask the second delivery specialist to execute the seller's hardest recurring task while the seller observes without intervening.
Have the company own the accounting tenant, domain, repository, and bank administration; give contractors revocable named access.
Run a five-business-day owner-absence test before adding management headcount, then cost every unresolved exception.

sections.heading: 2. Pay contractors for accepted outputs and review seven weekly signals
paragraphs: Contractor economics should purchase defined outputs, not conceal supervised employee hours. An illustrative Base allocation is $1,500 monthly for bookkeeping, $2,000 monthly for a bounded automation backlog, and $1,000 monthly for independent quality review: $54,000 annually in aggregate. These are proposed operating budgets inside the canonical cost envelope, not additional deductions from its published profit. Replace them with written quotations after inspecting transaction volume, system complexity, and technical requirements. Bookkeeping acceptance requires reconciled accounts and linked support by business day seven; automation acceptance requires passing tests, company repository delivery, and a demonstrated rollback; quality review acceptance requires documented sampling, severity classification, and corrective action evidence. Specify a two-business-day routine response target, while pricing urgent coverage separately rather than assuming constant availability. Pay monthly service fees against accepted recurring scope and milestone fees against accepted project deliverables. Include a defined cure period and objective rework responsibility, with payment timing consistent with applicable law. Worker status follows the actual relationship, including control and applicable federal and state tests, not the invoice label. Review 26 U.S.C. section 3121(d), wage obligations under 29 U.S.C. section 207, and relevant state classification rules before treating a recurring seat as independent.

Hold one weekly operating meeting using a locked scorecard extracted at the same cutoff each Monday. The controller owns definitions and reconciles financial measures; operating owners explain exceptions with source records, not presentation slides. Review seven signals: accepted revenue against plan, gross contribution by service cohort, delivery reliability, repeat-work defects, retention, concentration, and 13-week liquidity. Report numerator, denominator, comparison period, owner, and corrective action for each. Calculate delivery reliability as jobs accepted by the promised date divided by jobs due; do not remove late jobs by moving their dates after failure. Measure defects against completed work from the same cohort, including credits and unpaid rework. Retention should distinguish recurring-contract renewal from repeat purchasing in noncontract businesses. Review gross contribution after direct labor, materials, subcontractors, and attributable credits, while keeping interest outside that operating measure. A 98% on-time target and a 2% rework threshold are initial operating standards, not historical claims. Recalibrate only through a documented change that preserves prior-period comparability. Every red metric ends with one accountable person, a dated intervention, and evidence required for closure. A meeting that produces explanations but no changed operating action is overhead, not management.

Set a hard target of no more than 25% exposure to any customer group, measured separately on trailing-twelve-month recognized sales and open trade receivables. Aggregate related entities under common economic control; splitting invoices across subsidiaries does not diversify demand. Apply the same 25% ceiling to operating counterparties within each critical purchased-capacity category, and track customer referral intermediaries separately when they control demand access. Four equal suppliers leave no room for disruption, so five credible sources or genuinely substitutable capacity provide a more resilient design. Small businesses often inherit breaches: disclose them, stop increasing the dependency, and assign a dated remediation plan rather than pretending a temporary waiver meets the target. A buyer should see both current exposure and progress toward the ceiling. Track acquisition lenders and bank deposits in separate funding-risk schedules; these are not quietly included in an operating-supplier diversification claim. Stress-test the loss of the largest customer and interruption of the largest critical supplier in the cash forecast. Require verified alternative capacity, not a list of uncontacted vendors. Connect each resulting action to customer retention, capital structuring, or integration so the weekly scorecard remains tied to the seven mapped plays rather than becoming an unrelated reporting exercise.

Freeze dependency growth and execute dated account or supplier diversification

Opening cash plus collections less operating payments and debt service
Escalate projected cash shortfalls or any contractual covenant breach

sop_steps.action: Export accounting, CRM, job, and receivables records at Monday's agreed cutoff.

sections.heading: 3. Build accrual cohorts, transferable systems, and a defensible evidence room
paragraphs: Transferable books begin with an accrual ledger that distinguishes earned revenue, invoicing, and collections. Use QuickBooks Online or Xero with controlled account mapping, customer identifiers, service lines, and acquisition cohorts; the specific software matters less than consistent posting rules and exportability. Post customer deposits to liabilities until the relevant performance is delivered, and distinguish unbilled earned revenue from work that has not yet satisfied the recognition policy. Accrue received services, payroll, subcontractor work, and other incurred costs in the proper period. Reconcile bank accounts, receivables, payables, inventory where applicable, deferred revenue, fixed assets, and debt monthly. Business day seven is the initial close deadline, followed by controller review and period locking. Maintain a separate tax reconciliation rather than assuming management accrual treatment determines tax timing. Section 6001 of Title 26 requires supporting records, while section 461 addresses deduction timing subject to its applicable rules. Preserve invoice support and correction history so a QoE reviewer can reconstruct a period without interviewing the seller. Historical cash-basis accounts need a documented conversion bridge; changing software does not repair missing accruals. Treat unexplained opening balances as diligence exceptions with assigned resolution dates, not as permanent suspense accounts.

Use cohort accounting to expose acquisition damage that aggregate sales can conceal. Separate customers present at closing from customers won afterward, then segment by service line, contract type, and originating channel. Track recognized revenue, direct contribution, credits, renewal outcomes, and receivable aging within each cohort. A business can grow total sales while losing its acquired customer base and replacing it with lower-margin work. Reconcile cohort totals to the general ledger every month, with documented treatment for customer mergers and identifier changes. Build a monthly earnings bridge from reported operating results to proposed normalized earnings. Support every adjustment with invoices, payroll records, contracts, or a specific event. Recurring software, ordinary recruiting, routine repairs, and contractor costs are operating expenses even when the seller calls them discretionary. Replace owner labor at a defensible market cost before marketing manager-run earnings. Distinguish a genuinely completed integration project from continuing operational maintenance. Keep acquisition transaction costs and financing charges separately identifiable, with their accounting treatment reviewed rather than mechanically expensed or capitalized. This discipline supports quality of earnings, customer retention, and exit readiness simultaneously. It also gives the owner an actionable hold-case view: which customer cohorts actually fund debt service, replacement investment, and distributions after collection delays.

Control of operating assets must survive both contractor departure and an ownership change. Put automation scripts, templates, documentation, and proprietary process materials in company-controlled repositories with role-based access and tested exports. For copyright transfers, 17 U.S.C. section 204(a) generally requires a written instrument signed by the rights owner or an authorized agent. Do not assume paying an invoice transfers copyright, or that every commissioned work qualifies as work made for hire. Obtain assignments covering identified deliverables, and distinguish contractor pre-existing tools from newly created work. Where background technology remains contractor-owned, document a license sufficient for continued operation, modification, and the contemplated transfer. Maintain third-party license terms and dependency inventories; ownership of custom code does not eliminate restrictions in embedded components. Store signed customer and supplier contracts, assignment provisions, change-of-control clauses, permits, employment records, and lender documents in an indexed evidence room. Review SBA loan terms and applicable 13 CFR requirements before assuming an ownership transfer or asset disposition is permitted. Test that another authorized employee can restore the workflow and produce the monthly reports without the original contractor. A buyer discounts undocumented dependency even when the underlying code works, because operational continuity depends on enforceable rights and reproducible execution.

sections.heading: 4. Bridge canonical profit into buyer earnings and realizable owner cash
paragraphs: Keep the scorecard and valuation model separate but reconciled. Conservative recognized sales of $750,000 multiplied by 8% produce $60,000 annual owner profit; Base sales of $1,875,000 multiplied by 13.0% produce $243,750; Scaled sales of $3,000,000 multiplied by 18% produce $540,000. These are acquired-business sales, not customer GMV, transaction purchase price, loan proceeds, or an advisory fee pool. The margin basis is after interest and before principal repayments. Therefore none of these profit figures is automatically EBITDA or distributable cash. Start a buyer bridge with the actual definition of owner profit, then identify expensed interest, depreciation, amortization, applicable entity income taxes, owner compensation, and supported normalizations. If an expense was never deducted, adding it back manufactures earnings. Illustratively, assume Base profit includes $75,000 interest and $31,250 depreciation and amortization, includes market-rate compensation for all required owner duties, and includes no entity income-tax expense. Adding those two expenses produces $350,000 EBITDA before further adjustments. These are explicit bridge assumptions, not supplied scorecard facts. Validate them against the ledger before using the result. A buyer's replacement manager expense reduces normalized EBITDA whenever the assumed owner compensation does not actually cover the required duties.

Use multiple ranges as negotiation sensitivities, not as automatic rewards for clean folders. For a smaller owner-operated acquisition, an illustrative 2–3 times normalized seller discretionary earnings range may be a useful starting screen; SDE requires its own owner-benefit reconciliation and cannot be substituted for EBITDA. For a genuinely transferable small company, test 3–5 times normalized EBITDA, recognizing that size, industry, capital intensity, growth quality, concentration, and financing conditions can move outcomes outside that range. Obtain current comparable transactions and buyer indications before setting a reserve price. Applying 3, 4, and 5 times to the illustrative $350,000 EBITDA gives enterprise values of $1,050,000, $1,400,000, and $1,750,000. Those are not owner proceeds. At the middle sensitivity, subtract assumed bank debt of $600,000, seller-note principal of $150,000, and transaction costs of $70,000, then add $50,000 of transferable excess cash: estimated equity proceeds are $630,000 before taxes and any other adjustments. Define cash, debt-like items, and the working-capital peg in the transaction documents. Customer deposits, accrued bonuses, leases, and overdue payables require consistent treatment without double counting. Earnouts and rollover equity are contingent or illiquid consideration, not cash received at closing.

The durable cash-cow decision deserves the same rigor as the exit decision. Starting from Base owner profit of $243,750, an illustrative $90,000 annual principal schedule, $30,000 maintenance capital expenditure, and $20,000 working-capital increase leave $103,750 before owner-level taxes and other cash adjustments. Interest is already reflected in the scorecard profit, so subtracting it again understates cash. Conversely, ignoring principal exaggerates distributions. Calculate debt-service coverage using the precise lender definition and required measurement period; EBITDA divided by principal alone is not a complete coverage calculation. Compare holding cash flows with after-tax sale proceeds over an explicit horizon, including reinvestment, refinancing, owner time, and downside cases. Premium valuation becomes more plausible when the pod produces stable cohorts, independently reproducible reporting, low rework, bounded concentration, and an owner who is replaceable at a funded cost. None of those attributes changes the canonical scenario arithmetic by itself. Use the seven mapped plays as the operating loop: screening selects a staffable business; QoE verifies earnings; structuring protects liquidity; integration transfers decisions; retention preserves cohorts; automation reduces reporting friction; and exit readiness preserves strategic choice. Sell when actual buyer terms exceed a disciplined hold value, or retain the company when verified cash generation compensates for its continuing capital and labor demands.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #13, Business Acquisition, ranks #17 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 86/100 because purchased cash flow still requires capital, operators, and disciplined debt service. This sprint activates seven mapped plays: sourcing, screening, QoE, capital structuring, transaction execution, transition, and operating automation. Protect the seven-employee, three-contractor operating pod with staged diligence, a $12,000 first-month search ceiling, and explicit Day 30/60/90 decisions. Kill unsupported transactions, fix bounded evidence gaps, and scale only repeatable sourcing and verified operating economics.

sections.heading: 1. Days 1–7: Define the Buy Box, Staff the Pod, and Ring-Fence Cash
paragraphs: Start the clock when the sponsor authorizes the search, not when a seller accepts an offer. Candidate #13 typically requires 4–10 months to reach a first deal, so a successful opening month produces a qualified pipeline, documented underwriting, and a funded next stage rather than purchased revenue. Map the work into seven explicit chapter plays: P1 proprietary and broker sourcing; P2 buy-box screening; P3 Quality of Earnings; P4 SBA, conventional, and seller-note structuring; P5 diligence and transaction execution; P6 employee and customer transition; and P7 reporting automation and operating improvement. Assign each record one current play, one owner, one next action, and one evidence link in Airtable or HubSpot. On Day 1, write the acquisition thesis around service geography, recurring demand, transferable licenses, customer concentration, and manager replacement cost. On Day 2, convert the thesis into a rejection checklist and score ten historical listings. Reject a thesis that works only by treating the seller's unpaid labor as free capacity. Record the required operator salary before estimating debt capacity, and distinguish businesses worth investigating from businesses the sponsor can actually fund without consuming the operating reserve.

The canonical Conservative and Base operating configuration is seven full-time employees plus three contractors, not ten new search hires. Use seven employee seats for general management, accounting coordination, sales and account retention, service scheduling, and three delivery roles. Use the three contractor seats for a transaction attorney, a CPA with QoE capability, and an industry specialist covering systems and license transfer. These are functional assignments for a suitable target; map them to actual people before an offer and do not assume every industry supports this organization. Before closing, the sponsor performs sourcing and coordinates staged contractor work; target employees remain under the seller's authority. Request information through authorized seller channels rather than assigning work to staff the buyer does not employ. On Day 3, create a responsibility register showing which tasks become buyer responsibilities only at closing. On Day 4, obtain written contractor scopes with hour caps and exclusions. On Day 5, test a seller package handoff using a redacted sample. Require P3 findings to reach P4 underwriting and P6 staffing assumptions through the same versioned model, preventing separate teams from quietly using different earnings.

Authorize an illustrative $12,000 first-month search ceiling inside the $30,000–$120,000 startup-capital envelope, without implying that its lower end funds every target. Allocate $1,500 to data and outreach, $2,000 to initial legal review, $4,000 to limited accounting diligence, $1,000 to lender packaging, $1,000 to site visits, and $2,500 to contingency. Measure the ceiling as cash already paid plus noncancelable commitments, so an unpaid engagement letter cannot hide spending. Keep purchase equity, closing costs, and operating liquidity in separate ledger categories. The quoted $6,000–$25,000 monthly opex range is a planning input, not the complete expense bridge behind every revenue scenario; verify payroll, direct costs, debt service, and working capital separately. On Day 6, build a thirteen-week cash forecast and tag every proposed commitment to a play. On Day 7, reconcile the forecast with bank balances and contractor scopes. Stop discretionary commitments at 80% of the month ceiling, or $9,600, until remaining work is reprioritized. Never raid the target's payroll reserve to preserve a search schedule or keep an unpromising seller conversation alive.

callout.title: Four Pre-Flight Tests Before Paid Diligence Expands
callout.body: Release only the next evidence-producing tranche. A promising listing does not justify funding the entire transaction workstream.
items: Verify sponsor liquidity with current account evidence; separate acquisition equity from search spending and the thirteen-week operating reserve.
Confirm a named owner for each of the seven plays and a feasible seven-employee, three-contractor target organization before assuming labor savings.
Obtain a seller-authorized document channel, confidentiality terms, and written limits on customer or employee contact before collecting sensitive operating records.
Require capped CPA and attorney scopes plus an updated commitment ledger showing first-month search exposure no greater than $12,000.

sections.heading: 2. Days 8–14: Build a Qualified Funnel and Reconstruct Earnings
paragraphs: On Day 8, assemble 120 deduplicated prospects from broker listings, industry directories, referral partners, and targeted owner research. Distinguish a researched record from a contacted owner and a received package from a qualified opportunity. On Day 9, send twenty personalized first contacts; on Day 10, send twenty more and schedule broker calls. Describe the actual buy box, capital readiness, and management plan without implying committed financing. On Day 11, review responses and request confidentiality agreements only where the seller fits the thesis. On Day 12, seek eight usable packages containing three years of income statements, current year-to-date results, monthly sales, customer concentration, employee roles, and asking terms. Eight packages is an operating target, not a promised response rate. On Day 13, screen every available package using the same criteria; on Day 14, select up to three for deeper work. Record missing documents as specific requests with owners and dates rather than filling model cells with invented values. Keep seller-facing activity under P1, qualification under P2, and paid reconstruction under P3, so a growing contact count cannot masquerade as an expanding investable pipeline.

Reconstruct earnings from source records before negotiating on a seller's multiple. Export monthly general-ledger detail from QuickBooks Online or Xero where authorized, then tie reported sales to bank deposits, merchant settlements, accounts-receivable movements, and sales-tax liabilities. Deposits are corroboration, not a substitute for revenue recognition: loan proceeds, owner transfers, customer prepayments, and collected taxes must not become acquired-business sales. Inspect at least three recent months and the prior year-end bridge during the limited review, then expand the period when seasonality or exceptions justify full QoE. Build an add-back schedule with evidence, recurrence assessment, replacement cost, and proposed lender treatment. An owner's salary is not entirely discretionary when the seven-person employee pod still needs a general manager. Challenge related-party rent against a sustainable lease and replace missing maintenance with a realistic expense. Treat an unexplained revenue reconciliation difference above 2% of the tested period's sales as a Fix trigger, not proof of misconduct. Require a dated explanation within ten business days; falsified records or a refusal to provide material support instead justify killing that transaction.

Preserve the scorecard while testing each target against it. Conservative annual sales of $750,000 at 8% produce $60,000 owner net profit; Base sales of $1,875,000 at 13.0% produce $243,750; Scaled sales of $3,000,000 at 18% produce $540,000. These are acquired operating-business revenues, not purchase prices, loan principal, or transaction values. Monthly arithmetic equivalents are $62,500 sales and $5,000 profit; $156,250 sales and $20,312.50 profit; and $250,000 sales and $45,000 profit. Use those equivalents only as comparison lines, since actual collections may be seasonal. All three profit cases are after interest and before principal repayments. For example, subtracting an illustrative $100,000 annual principal obligation from Base profit leaves $143,750 before other cash-flow adjustments; it does not establish distributable cash. Prepare separate bridges for depreciation, capital expenditure, working capital, and applicable taxes. Do not force an expensive acquisition into the Base case by deleting principal from the cash forecast or adding financing proceeds to revenue. The purchase model must show whether the required return survives the actual price, funding mix, replacement labor, and retained liquidity.

callout.title: Buy Evidence Before You Buy a Multiple
callout.body: Veteran buyers compress low-cost rejection work and preserve specialist hours for discrepancies that can change price or ownership risk.
items: Ask for monthly sales before the polished presentation; seasonality and sudden quarter-end spikes determine which bank and receivable periods deserve inspection.
Price the seller's replacement role before debating discretionary add-backs; a departing owner who dispatches jobs and sells accounts represents two operating dependencies.
Send the same short lender package to a limited, tracked lender cohort; compare reserve requirements and seller-note treatment instead of collecting vague borrowing estimates.
Maintain a rejected-deal ledger with reasons and evidence; recurring license-transfer or customer-concentration failures are signals to repair the thesis, not increase outreach blindly.

sections.heading: 3. Days 15–21: Price Debt, Expose Transfer Risk, and Design the Handoff
paragraphs: On Day 15, build a sources-and-uses model for each surviving target including price, fees, inventory treatment, working-capital delivery, equity, senior debt, and any seller note. On Day 16, request written preliminary lender feedback on borrower eligibility, business eligibility, equity, liquidity, collateral, and seller-note terms. SBA lending requires attention to 13 CFR 120.110 and 120.150, together with current program procedures and the lender's actual credit requirements. Do not assume a seller note automatically counts as equity or may receive current payments. On Day 17, stress the proposed capital structure with sales down 15%, direct-cost ratios unchanged, fixed cash costs unchanged, and floating borrowing rates up two percentage points. Calculate debt service coverage as consistently defined cash available for debt service divided by scheduled cash interest plus principal on all payable debt. This chapter's underwriting hurdles are at least 1.35 times in the base underwriting case and 1.10 times under stress; they are internal policy choices, not universal SBA thresholds. Use the stricter applicable lender covenant when it differs, and document how standby debt, leases, owner compensation, and taxes enter the lender's calculation.

On Day 18, have the attorney map transfer risks across assets, equity, contracts, licenses, employee obligations, and tax accounts. Search applicable UCC filing offices using verified debtor names and jurisdictions, then obtain payoff and release mechanics rather than assuming an asset purchase erases liens. UCC 9-315 generally preserves a security interest after disposition unless the secured party authorizes a disposition free of it or another rule applies; the controlling state's enactment matters. On Day 19, prepare a transaction-specific diligence index with dated requests for tax filings, litigation, payroll liabilities, permits, leases, insurance claims, and material contracts. In a qualifying asset acquisition, Internal Revenue Code section 1060 requires purchase-price allocation using the applicable residual method; align the agreement and Form 8594 reporting. A letter of intent should identify the intended structure, working-capital mechanism, evidence conditions, exclusivity period, and treatment of seller debt without pretending the final allocation is already resolved. Kill a transaction if a required license cannot transfer or be replaced on an acceptable timetable. Fix a documentable release or consent gap only when a responsible party accepts a dated, verifiable cure.

On Day 20, draft the first hundred days of ownership without exercising control before closing. Identify the ten largest customers, every single-person process dependency, and the employees needed for payroll, scheduling, billing, and delivery continuity. Obtain seller permission before customer or employee contact, and use aggregated data where individual records are unnecessary. On Day 21, test the proposed handoff against the seven employee and three contractor seats. The general manager owns P6 transition, the accounting coordinator owns P7 reporting, and the industry specialist supports systems migration without becoming an invisible permanent employee. Reconcile employment authorization procedures with 8 U.S.C. 1324a and transaction-specific successor practices; employee records need restricted access and clear custody. Keep payroll, banking, and customer communications unchanged until authorized transition steps are ready. Automate a read-only weekly reporting pack before changing invoicing or bank permissions. The minimum pack shows collected cash, receivable aging, gross margin, scheduled debt service, and thirteen-week liquidity. A target requiring a permanent eleventh person at Base economics needs a revised model or a lower price, not an unexplained headcount exception hidden inside a contractor invoice.
